item.title: Biomimetic Fabrication and Osteogenic Efficacy Evaluation of Tilapia-Derived Collagen-Based Artificial Bone Scaffolds
item.description:
Abstract
Inspired by the natural biomineralization processes observed in terrestrial vertebrates, this study independently designed an in vitro mineralization system to activate nucleation sites within tilapia fish collagen, facilitating the fabrication of biomimetic bone substitutes. Through lyophilization and molding techniques, a three-dimensional porous scaffold with a defined spatial architecture and adequate mechanical integrity was successfully constructed. Subsequently, the physicochemical properties, biocompatibility, and biodegradation characteristics of the prepared fish collagen-based artificial bone (FC-AB) were evaluated and compared to relevant standards. Furthermore, a rat tibial critical-sized defect model was employed to assess the in vivo bone regeneration capacity. The results demonstrated that the FC-AB scaffold possesses an ideal porous microstructure, excellent biocompatibility, and controllable degradation characteristics. Notably, it significantly promoted the osteogenesis and functional restoration of the bone defect. In conclusion, this research confirms the feasibility of utilizing fish collagen as a precursor for in vitro mineralization, yielding artificial bone materials with superior structural mimicry, mechanical competence, and osteoinductive potential, thereby positioning it as a promising candidate for bone tissue engineering.

item.title: Synergistic Absorption Mechanism in Flexible Polymer Composites Reinforced with Rare Earth Cobaltite and Molybdenum Carbide for EMI Shielding Applications
item.description:
Abstract
The sudden growth of digital devices and fifth-generation (5G) communication systems has generated increasing concerns regarding electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding in advanced technological applications, due to the high necessity for development of flexible, lightweight and efficient shielding materials. In this study, low thickness polymer composite films based on poly(vinylidene fluoride) polymer that is incorporated with gadolinium cobaltite and molybdenum carbide fillers were successfully fabricated through a solution casting technique. The chemical, structural, and morphological characteristics of the composite films were investigated using XRD, FTIR, FESEM, HR-TEM, tensile strength and contact angle. Thermal stability was assessed through thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and electromagnetic properties were evaluated in terms of complex permittivity and permeability across the X-band frequency range. The EMI shielding was examined in terms of shielding effectiveness due to absorption, reflection, and transmission and further validated using CST software. The selected composite film with an ultralow thickness of ∼0.15 mm exhibited a maximum EMI shielding efficiency of ∼49 dB in the X-band region with the absorption dominant shielding as the primary attenuation mechanism. The composite films displayed an enhanced mechanical strength and hydrophobicity behavior, making them suitable for flexible and durable shielding applications. These results suggest that the developed PVDF/GdCoO3/Mo2C composite films are promising candidates for advanced electromagnetic interference shielding applications in wearable electronics, stealth technology, and defense systems.

item.title: Terbium-Doped Graphene Quantum Dots: A Highly Efficient and Selective Fluorescent Nanoprobe for Vanillin Detection
item.description:
Abstract
Vanillin, an extensively used flavoring compound in our daily life, may lead to health problems when overused, adulterated, or poorly controlled in commercial settings, necessitating the development of sensitive and rapid detection techniques. In this work, terbium-doped graphene quantum dots (Tb-GQD) were synthesized using carbonization and chemical conjugation methods for developing an efficient fluorescent probe for vanillin detection. The structural and optical characteristics of Tb-GQD confirm that terbium is doped in GQDs, without disturbing the sp2 graphitic core of GQD, and efficient energy transfer from GQD to Tb3+ was observed from the photoluminescence emission studies. Upon addition of vanillin to Tb-GQD, a decrease in fluorescence emission intensity and a change in lifetime were observed, suggesting a dynamic, photoinduced electron transfer mechanism. The Tb-GQD shows a linear detection range of 0.2–85 μM with a detection limit of 13.2 nM. The synthesized fluorescent probe shows excellent selectivity, and was implemented in real-sample analysis with a good recovery range of 96.4–100.06% and an RSD below 3.6%. These findings show that Tb-GQD will serve as an efficient platform for detecting vanillin.

item.title: Hydrogel Formulation Containing PLGA Nanoparticles for Controlled Codelivery of Vitamin D and Chlorhexidine as a Promising Approach for Postdental Implant Applications
item.description:
Abstract
Tooth loss can have a significant impact on oral health and quality of life, and dental implants are currently the standard option for its replacement. However, implant failure still occurs, with bacterial infection and inadequate osseointegration being the most common causes. In this context, vitamin D3 was selected for its known pro-osteogenic role, while chlorhexidine (CHX), a widely used antiseptic with recognized bactericidal and bacteriostatic activity, was chosen as the antimicrobial component. To enable controlled and localized delivery of both molecules, two types of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles (NPs) were developed, CHX- and vitamin D3-loaded NPs. The produced NPs displayed an average size of 140 nm, a polydispersity index below 0.2, and negative ζ-potentials. Encapsulation efficiency reached 39% for CHX and 98% for vitamin D3, and transmission electron microscopy confirmed their spherical morphology. In vitro release assays demonstrated an initial burst release followed by a slower release phase for 3 days under simulated physiological conditions, while stability tests under storage conditions showed preservation of the nanoformulations’ physicochemical properties for at least 2 months. Antibacterial assays against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) and Staphylococcus epidermidis (S. epidermidis) confirmed the antimicrobial effect of CHX-loaded NPs. Cytotoxicity studies in human dermal fibroblasts indicated that combining both formulations (50 nM vitamin D3 and 0.01% w/v CHX) was safe. To facilitate application in the oral cavity, the NP mixture was incorporated into a nontoxic, pseudoplastic hydrogel. These findings highlight the potential of this nanohydrogel as a localized therapeutic approach capable of providing localized antimicrobial activity and supporting conditions favorable to osseointegration, paving the way for improved long-term implant outcomes.

item.title: Pro-Apoptotic and Autophagy-Inducing Activity of Novel 1,4-Naphthoquinone Derivatives against Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma without ROS Generation
item.description:
Abstract
Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains a major global health burden, and current platinum-based chemotherapeutics are constrained by systemic toxicity and acquired resistance, motivating the search for novel antitumor agents. Naphthoquinones are a privileged scaffold in anticancer drug discovery. Here, we report the synthesis of 18 1,4-naphthoquinone esters (1–18), 14 of which are novel, and their first evaluation as anticancer agents against three OSCC cell lines (SCC-4, SCC-9, and SCC-25) and primary human gingival fibroblasts. Derivative 14 emerged as the lead compound, displaying a geometric mean IC50 of 5.0 μM and a geometric mean selectivity index of 9.15, outperforming, in terms of selectivity, the chemotherapeutic standards carboplatin, lapachol, and shikonin. Mechanistically, 14 induced cell death through a combined apoptotic–autophagic pathway, evidenced by membrane blebbing, G2/M arrest, sub-G1 DNA fragmentation, caspase 3/7 activation, and LC3-puncta formation, with wortmannin-mediated rescue indicating that autophagy contributes to cell death, and without detectable induction of reactive oxygen species. This phenotype was accompanied by pronounced disorganization of the actin and tubulin cytoskeletal networks, evidenced by confocal fluorescence microscopy and reduced anisotropy of both networks. Derivative 14 induced less than 5% hemolysis at concentrations up to 1000 μM and was well tolerated in C57BL/6 mice at intraperitoneal doses up to 600 mg/kg, with no mortality or morphological alterations. In silico analyses showed no violations of Lipinski’s rule of five and a topological polar surface area within the range associated with good membrane permeability, while reverse molecular docking pointed to the DNA-binding domains of topoisomerase IIα and IIβ as plausible molecular targets, with binding modes and energies comparable to doxorubicin. Together, these findings establish 14 as a selective and well-tolerated 1,4-naphthoquinone derivative, with a proposed mechanism of action, warranting further preclinical development against OSCC.

item.title: Environment-Aware Deep Learning for Adaptive Dissolved Oxygen Sensing: Resolving the Information Efficiency Paradox in Aquatic Monitoring
item.description:
Abstract
Continuous high-frequency monitoring of dissolved oxygen (DO) faces a fundamental conflict between excessive energy consumption and substantial data redundancy, whereas conventional fixed-frequency sampling risks frequency aliasing and the omission of acute transient ecological events. To resolve this dilemma, a knowledge-guided, seasonally adaptive dynamic sampling strategy coupled with bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) reconstruction is proposed. Validated via long-term datasets from two hydrodynamically distinct Yangtze River stations, this framework yields three principal findings. First, summer precipitation acts as the primary catalyst for acute hypoxic risks (DO < 5.0 mg/L), whereas winter rainfall predominantly drives reaeration, dictating the nonstationary triggers for dynamic sampling. Second, optimal data decimation exhibits pronounced spatial heterogeneity governed by site-specific environmental buffering capacities; high-fidelity reconstruction requires merely 22.99% data retention at the hydrodynamically stable Nanjinguan mainstream. Third, a counterintuitive information efficiency paradox is mathematically proven at the highly volatile Chenglingji lake outlet: the dynamic strategy (utilizing 50.23% of data) achieves a Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) of 0.969, vastly outperforming the uncompressed 100% full-data baseline (KGE = 0.797). This confirms that environmentally triggered sparse sampling intrinsically functions as an adaptive nonlinear filter, actively stripping stochastic environmental noise to prevent algorithmic overfitting. Ultimately, integrating physical priors into data acquisition resolves the energy-fidelity trade-off, establishing a highly resilient, low-power architectural foundation for autonomous basin-scale aquatic monitoring networks under escalating climatic extremes.

item.title: Responses of Fibroblasts, Mesenchymal Stem Cells, and Macrophages after Irradiation with Proton and Silver Ion Emission Guns under Atmospheric Pressure
item.description:
Abstract
Various approaches have been developed to regulate cell growth using physiological or physical stimuli. In this study, we focused on ion implantation technology, which has the potential to deliver both types of stimuli. We developed an ion gun capable of releasing protons or silver ions (Ag+) under atmospheric pressure conditions and used it to irradiate mouse fibroblasts (NIH3T3), mouse mesenchymal stem cells (KUSA-A1), and mouse macrophages (RAW264), evaluating their respective responses. Cell viability decreased with increasing doses of ions emitted from the proton gun. Conversely, high doses of ions emitted from the Ag+ gun reduced the metabolic activity of all the cell types, but low doses enhanced that of RAW264 cells. Thus, the effects varied among ion species, even at nearly equivalent doses, indicating distinct cellular responses depending on the ion provided by the guns. Evaluation of osteogenic differentiation after irradiation with a proton gun in KUSA-A1 cells revealed that low doses of ions emitted from the proton gun promoted alkaline phosphatase activity, while high doses inhibited it. This biphasic response suggests that changes in intracellular pH and energy transfer may contribute to the observed response, warranting further investigations.

item.title: Experimental Study on the Synthesis of Molybdenum Disulfide Quantum Dots by Ultrasonic, Solvent-Thermal, and Atmospheric Plasma-Assisted Exfoliation
item.description:
Abstract
Molybdenum disulfide quantum dots (MoS2 QDs) were synthesized using ultrasonic (US), solvent-thermal (ST), and atmospheric plasma-assisted (PA) top-down exfoliation. Energy analysis shows PA exfoliation is remarkably more energy-efficient and faster due to direct plasma-precursor contact. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) indicated average particle sizes of 4.95 nm (ST), 5.59 nm (US), and 8.69 nm (PA). All samples exhibited strong UV-blue and broad red-to-NIR absorption. The QDs displayed excitation-dependent photoluminescence, with PA samples showing twice the emission intensity of US and ST versions. Across all methods, functional performance was comparable: an 808 nm laser-induced photothermal heating in water to 47 °C within 5 min, while UV irradiation triggered >50% methyl orange photocatalytic degradation within 40 min. This indicates that functional behavior is inherently governed by the QDs rather than the synthesis route. Consequently, highly efficient PA exfoliation offers a promising, scalable pathway for producing multifunctional MoS2 QDs.

item.title: Developing a Quantum Physics-Inspired Machine Learning Model for Partition Coefficient Prediction and Comparing Its Performance with Empirical Descriptors and Molecular Graph-Based Models
item.description:
Abstract
Predicting the partition coefficient (logP) is critical in pharmaceutical research for assessing the bioavailability of small molecules. We present a novel quantum physics-inspired machine learning model (QM-ML) for predicting logP and compare its performance with an empirical descriptor-based model and a graph neural network (GNN) model. For all the models investigated, feature selection was conducted to refine the high-dimensional descriptor space and identify critical determinants of lipophilicity or logP. Quantum mechanical descriptors, in particular frontier orbital energies derived, such as chemical potential, hardness, electrophilicity, electronegativity, and dipole moment, transfer energy, and quantum mechanical polar surface area (QMPSA), were extracted to construct QM-ML mod. The results indicate that the hybrid model achieved the highest predictive accuracy, yielding an R2 of 0.9248, a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.3511, and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.4981. The ExtraTrees regressor, utilizing empirical classical Mordred descriptors, demonstrated comparable performance with an R2 of 0.9141. While models relying exclusively on frontier orbital energies showed limited accuracy (R2 = 0.4349), the inclusion of explicit solvation energy (ΔG) and QMPSA significantly improved the physics-based model performance (R2 = 0.8132). The DeepChem-based GCN model also achieved an R2 of 0.8936. Notably, the explainability analysis showed that certain QM descriptors, such as solvation energy (ΔG) and non-polar QMPSA, contributed significantly to the model performance. The hybrid model outperformed all the physics-based and baseline Mordred models with large-scale descriptor sets and showed the importance of certain QM descriptors, such as solvation transfer energy and QM-PSA. These findings highlight the potential of a hybrid data-driven model involving physics-based descriptors to capture complex molecular interactions and underscore the importance of targeted feature engineering in quantitative structure–property relationship modeling.

item.title: Integrated Whole-Cell Phage Display and Machine Learning Identify Candidate Targeting Ligands in KRAS-Defined Lung Cancer Contexts
item.description:
Abstract
Phage display can identify ligands that target distinctive cell surface phenotypes, but selection outputs are often complex and difficult to interpret. Here, we developed an integrated workflow combining phage display biopanning, next-generation sequencing (NGS), machine learning (ML), and flow cytometry to discover short peptide binders associated with genotype-defined cancer contexts. Phage display was performed on lung cancer cell lines representing KRAS wild-type (WT), G12C, G12D, and G12V backgrounds, and experimental outputs were used to train a multimodal probabilistic model. From the resulting model-generated candidates, 98 nonredundant heptapeptides were selected for synthesis, and 88 were successfully solubilized and tested experimentally. Flow cytometry validation revealed heterogeneous binding behaviors, including broad pan-cellular binders and candidates with mutant-vs-WT binding preference. Extended dose–response profiling and normal-cell counter-screening enabled prioritization based on binding magnitude, curve behavior, normal-cell reactivity, and sequence developability. Overall, this study shows how whole-cell selection data sets can be analyzed computationally and experimentally to identify and prioritize peptide candidates for targeting strategies.

item.title: Bismuth-Catalyzed Multifunctional Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) Composites with Tunable Thermomechanical Properties for Scalable Manufacturing
item.description:
Abstract
Bismuth-catalyzed silicone systems have recently emerged as promising eco-friendly alternatives to conventional tin- and platinum-based catalysts; however, their behavior in highly filled, scalable composite formulations remains insufficiently understood. In this work, multifunctional polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composites were developed using a bismuth carboxylate catalyst and two structurally distinct inorganic fillers, perlite and hollow glass microspheres (GMBs), to systematically investigate structure–processing–property relationships and enable tunable thermomechanical performance. Rheological analysis revealed that filler incorporation significantly alters curing behavior, with gelation temperatures increasing from ∼105 °C for neat PDMS to ∼155 °C (+50 °C) for 40 wt % perlite and ∼162 °C (+57 °C) for 40 wt % GMBs, enabling extended processing windows critical for scalable manufacturing. Thermomechanical characterization demonstrated that filler type, through its morphology, intrinsic density, and resulting volume fraction, governs property evolution. Perlite enhanced through-thickness thermal conductivity by up to 42% (0.193 to 0.274 W·m–1·K–1), whereas GMBs reduced thermal conductivity by 47% (to 0.102 W·m–1·K–1), enabling bidirectional thermal transport tuning within a single material platform. Significant reductions in coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) were achieved, reaching 43% (perlite) and 74% (GMBs), while density decreased to <0.65 g·cm–3 for GMB-filled systems, highlighting lightweighting potential. Mechanical performance was substantially improved, with compressive modulus increasing by 339% for perlite-filled composites and up to 1889% for GMB-filled systems, alongside a ∼255% (∼3.6×) higher compressive strength than the perlite-filled composite at the highest filler content. Importantly, the bismuth-catalyzed PDMS formulations exhibited robust scalability, demonstrated through successful sheet molding compound (SMC) processing and compression molding of kilogram-scale, fiber-reinforced composite structures with excellent dimensional stability and flame resistance. These results establish bismuth-catalyzed PDMS composites as a versatile, environmentally benign materials platform with tailorable properties. The findings provide critical insights into filler–matrix–cure interactions and offer a pathway toward the design of next-generation silicone composites for thermal management, lightweight structures, building materials, and large-scale industrial manufacturing.

item.title: Co 2 (OH) 3 Cl/Nb 2 CT x : Advanced Composite Electrodes for High-Performance Aqueous Asymmetric Supercapacitors
item.description:
Abstract
Cobalt hydroxy chloride-based mixed anionic frameworks are attracting attention as supercapacitor electrode materials because of their high theoretical capacity and enhanced redox-active cobalt centers with increased interlayer spacing. on the other hand, Nb2CTx MXene provides conductive, hydrophilic, multivalent Nb that improves electronic transport and maintains good structural stability during electrochemical reactions. In this work, Co2(OH)3Cl/Nb2CTx composites containing 1, 3, and 5 wt % Nb2CTx relative to the mass of Co2(OH)3Cl were synthesized. Further, the specific electrochemical characteristics of the as-prepared composite and bare sample were evaluated using a three-electrode configuration. We fabricated asymmetric supercapacitors using the as-prepared materials as the positive electrode and activated carbon as the negative electrode, with PVA–KOH gel as the electrolyte. The asymmetric supercapacitor fabricated using CN-1 delivered a specific capacity of 158.81 C g–1 at 1 A g–1 and showed a maximum specific energy of 35.29 Wh kg–1 at a specific power of 1.6 kW kg–1. The composite electrode-based device showed an enhanced cycle life of up to 20,000 cycles, with 76.7% capacitance retention and a Coulombic efficiency of around 99%. In contrast, the bare Co2(OH)3Cl-based device retained about 50.6% capacitance after 20,000 cycles. Thus, the optimistic Co2(OH)3Cl/Nb2CTx composites are a potential positive electrode for high-performance supercapacitor applications.

item.title: Taguchi L8 Optimization of Processing Conditions in Designing a Functional Food Product: An Antioxidant-Rich Tomato Soup with Preserved Melatonin-Serotonin- l -Tryptophan Synergy
item.description:
Abstract
The indoleamine antioxidant triad (melatonin, serotonin, and l-tryptophan) displayed in vivo bioavailabilities in rat models when delivered through a tomato-based soup. The present study focuses on the development of this antioxidant-rich tomato-based soup (with preserved antioxidant synergy) through rigorous optimization of processing conditions and comprehensive physicochemical characterization of the finished product, including proximate composition and rheological properties. A Taguchi L8 (eight experimental combinations) orthogonal experimental design was employed to investigate the effects of processing temperature (50–60 °C), guar gum concentration (0.25–0.35%), and processing time (8–10 min) on indoleamine retention and antioxidant synergy effect (SE). Signal-to-noise ratio analysis (larger-the-better criterion) indicated that processing time exerted the most significant influence on indoleamine stability (F = 227.5 for melatonin; F = 171.1 for serotonin; p < 0.05); whereas, temperature and guar gum concentration showed comparatively lesser effects. The optimized processing conditions─processing temperature of 60 °C, addition of 0.35% guar gum, and processing time of 8 min─resulted in maximum retention of melatonin (6.85 μg g–1 dwb), serotonin (17.12 μg g–1 dwb), and l-tryptophan (22.43 μg g–1 dwb) in the designer tomato soup. The same also demonstrated effective preservation of indoleamine stability and antioxidant synergy (SE value 1.01).

item.title: Machine Learning-Driven Comparative Prediction of Compressive Strength in True Geopolymer and Hybrid Alkali-Activated Cement Systems
item.description:
Abstract
Ordinary Portland cement (OPC) production accounts for approximately 7–8% of global CO2 emissions, motivating the development of sustainable binders such as metakaolin-based geopolymers and hybrid alkali-activated cements (AACs). However, accurate prediction of compressive strength in these systems remains challenging because of nonlinear interactions among precursor composition, activator chemistry, water-related parameters, and curing conditions. This study develops a reliability-oriented machine-learning framework using literature-derived datasets comprising 223 metakaolin-based geopolymer mixtures and 262 hybrid AAC mixtures. Five tree-based ensemble algorithms were evaluated using five-fold GroupKFold validation, with literature source used as the grouping variable to reduce the risk of study-level information leakage. The framework further incorporated fold-wise hyperparameter optimization, inverse-frequency sample weighting during model fitting, source-wise sensitivity analysis, and leave-one-source-out evaluation. Under grouped internal validation, CatBoost achieved the best performance for the metakaolin-based geopolymer dataset (R2 = 0.8211 ± 0.1275, RMSE = 5.773 ± 2.333 MPa, MAE = 4.131 ± 1.543 MPa), whereas Gradient Boosting performed best for the hybrid AAC dataset (R2 = 0.8876 ± 0.0708, RMSE = 3.333 ± 1.181 MPa, MAE = 2.366 ± 0.737 MPa). TreeSHAP analysis revealed distinct model-derived feature associations: hybrid AAC predictions were most strongly associated with GGBFS content, followed by activator- and curing-related variables, whereas metakaolin-based geopolymer predictions were most strongly associated with the H2O/Na2O ratio, aggregate proportion, activator chemistry, and curing conditions. These SHAP-derived patterns represent statistical associations learned by the models rather than direct evidence of physical causation or reaction mechanisms. Overall, the proposed framework provides a transparent approach for preliminary compressive-strength screening and experimental prioritization of sustainable alkali-activated binders.

item.title: Balancing Carbon Percolation and MnO 2 Pseudocapacitance in a Few-Layer Graphite/Carbon Black Waterborne Ink for Screen-Printed Planar Microsupercapacitors
item.description:
Abstract
Waterborne conductive inks for screen-printed planar microsupercapacitors (MSCs) must reconcile low-cost processing, print fidelity, electronic conduction, and electrochemical activity. Graphite/carbon black (CB) networks provide scalable conduction but limited charge storage, whereas excessive manganese dioxide (MnO2) can disrupt electron and ion pathways. Here, we identify a practical composition window, within the tested range, for a ternary few-layer graphite (F-GT)/CB/MnO2 ink prepared by high-speed dispersion and planetary ball milling. F-GT forms the long-range conductive scaffold, CB bridges interflake junctions, and MnO2 supplies pseudocapacitive sites without dominating the percolated carbon network. The optimized ink exhibited shear-thinning behavior and reproduced fine patterns on paper and PET. At an F-GT/CB/MnO2 mass ratio of 5:1:3, screen-printed MSCs with a PVA/LiCl gel electrolyte delivered 19.7 mF cm–2 and 9.95 F cm–3 and 1.34 F g–1 at 0.05 mA cm–2 and 2.73 μWh cm–2 at 0.025 mW cm–2. The devices retained 83.7% of their capacitance after 5000 charge–discharge cycles and 90.5% after 1000 bending cycles. Three series-connected devices operated at 3 V and powered a green light-emitting diode. These results show how MnO2 loading can add oxide-based charge storage while preserving a low-cost graphite-derived conductive framework for flexible printed energy storage.

item.title: Performance and Degradation Behavior of Coconut and Sisal Fibers Exposed to Alkaline Solutions and Embedded in Concrete Matrices
item.description:
Abstract
The use of natural lignocellulosic fibers as reinforcement in cementitious materials has attracted increasing interest because of their low environmental impact, renewability, and wide availability. However, the long-term durability of these fibers under highly alkaline conditions remains a major limitation for their application in cement-based composites. This study investigates the degradation behavior and performance of coconut and sisal fibers, under untreated and alkali-treated conditions, exposed to alkaline solutions and incorporated into concretes produced with two Portland cement types (PC V and PC IV). The experimental program included total organic carbon (TOC) analysis, gravimetric degradation tests under cyclic immersion conditions, Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and compressive strength tests of fiber-reinforced concretes. The results demonstrated that alkalinity is the main factor governing fiber degradation, promoting the dissolution of hemicellulose and lignin, cellulose depolymerization, and progressive microstructural deterioration. TOC analysis revealed substantially higher organic matter release under alkaline exposure compared with thermal treatment alone, confirming the strong susceptibility of lignocellulosic components to alkaline attack. Sisal fibers exhibited higher initial degradation due to their elevated cellulose content and lower lignin fraction, whereas coconut fibers showed a greater chemical stability. Alkali treatment reduced the mass loss during degradation cycles, particularly for sisal fibers, indicating partial stabilization through the removal of alkali-sensitive amorphous constituents. FT-IR analyses showed that cellulose-related bands near 1400 cm–1 and 1028–1052 cm–1 are sensitive indicators of alkaline degradation, especially for sisal fibers exposed to the simulated pore solution. SEM observations confirmed significant surface deterioration, microfibril separation, and increased roughness after alkaline exposure with treated fibers generally exhibiting lower structural damage than untreated fibers. In the concrete mixtures, coconut fibers demonstrated superior compatibility with both cement matrices, maintaining compressive strength values close to those of the reference concrete. Conversely, sisal fibers caused significant reductions in compressive strength, despite their intrinsically higher tensile properties, indicating that chemical durability and fiber stability govern composite performance more strongly than the isolated fiber strength. The results further indicate that the moderate reduction in alkalinity provided by PC IV cement is insufficient to prevent the degradation of cellulose-rich fibers. Overall, the study demonstrates that fiber composition and chemical stability are critical factors controlling the performance of natural fiber-reinforced cementitious composites, highlighting coconut fibers as a more promising alternative for applications in alkaline environments.

item.title: Phenolate-Mediated Structural Evolution of Lignin toward Hard Carbon Anodes for Sodium-Ion Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
Hard carbon (HC) anodes are typically described in terms of their final structure. However, this structure is influenced by multiple competing factors, and precursor-level chemical interactions can play an important role in directing its eventual evolution. Here, metal coordination is used to direct lignin precursor organization and control the evolution of lignin-derived HCs. Magnesium gluconate (MgGlu2) introduced into alkaline lignin promotes selective Mg2+ coordination with oxygen-containing functional groups, enabling reorganization of the lignin network prior to carbonization. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations show a thermodynamic preference of Mg2+ for phenolate (Ph–)-rich environments over gluconate ligands and β–O–4 linkages, consistent with the formation of cross-linked precursor configurations. This coordination is preserved during freeze-drying and translates into a distinct carbon microstructure upon pyrolysis. The resulting carbon exhibits a more accessible pore structure and improved cycling stability, retaining 93.6% of its post-solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) capacity after 400 cycles, compared to 8.7% for the pristine counterpart. These results demonstrate that phenolate-directed Mg2+ coordination governs precursor organization and contributes to the structural stability of lignin-derived HCs. More broadly, this work establishes precursor-level coordination as a route to control structure–performance relationships in HC anodes.

item.title: Toll-Like Receptors in Mycoplasma Infections: Immunopathogenesis, Cheminformatics, and Machine Learning-Based Insights into TLR-Targeted Therapeutics
item.description:
Abstract
Mycoplasma species are the minimal-genome pathogens that elicit complex host immune responses involving both protective and pathogenic inflammation. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are pivotal components of the immune system, recognizing pathogen-associated molecular patterns and damage-associated molecular patterns to initiate immune responses. TLRs recognize Mycoplasma-derived lipoproteins, glycolipids, and CpG-rich DNA motifs, initiating NF-κB and MAPK signaling cascades. While these pathways are indispensable for microbial clearance, their dysregulation contributes to chronic inflammation, autoimmunity, and tissue damage. Consequently, selective modulation of TLR signaling has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for restoring immune homeostasis. In this study, we summarized the recent advances in delineating the molecular crosstalk between TLRs and Mycoplasma, emphasizing the distinct roles of TLRs in pathogen recognition and immunopathology. In parallel, it integrates a cheminformatics-based analysis of TLR inhibitory ligands retrieved from the ChEMBL database, encompassing over 230 compounds across TLR1–5. Multivariate visualization techniques such as principal component analysis (PCA), uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), and t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) were employed to map the chemical space and reveal receptor-specific clustering patterns. The analysis identified TLR2 and TLR4 inhibitors as occupying distinct but overlapping chemical regions, characterized by higher molecular weight, lipophilicity, and structural complexity. Correlation and similarity mapping further highlighted scaffold conservation among active ligands, providing a quantitative foundation for rational drug design and structure–activity modeling. Furthermore, we explore how machine learning (ML) and computational modeling are reshaping TLR-targeted drug discovery. ML-driven frameworks facilitate ligand prediction, virtual screening, and structure–activity optimization through deep docking and transformer-based scoring models. Integrative ML approaches also extend beyond ligand discovery to encompass multiomics data integration, biomarker identification, and predictive modeling of host–pathogen interactions and immune responses. By bridging immunological insight with cheminformatics and ML-based analytics, this article outlines a multidisciplinary roadmap for precision immunomodulation in Mycoplasma-associated diseases. The convergence of experimental pharmacology and computational intelligence holds the potential to accelerate the discovery of next-generation TLR-targeted therapeutics, advancing personalized strategies for immune regulation and infection control.

item.title: Molecular Engineering of Sarcosine Oxidase and Horseradish Peroxidase: Impact of Lysine Accessibility on Covalent Bioconjugation and Bioelectrocatalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Sarcosine has emerged as a critical biomarker for the early diagnosis of prostate cancer, necessitating the development of highly sensitive and simplified electrochemical detection methods. While the bioconjugation of enzymes offers a pathway toward enhanced bioelectronic performance, biosensors based on bioconjugated sarcosine oxidase remain largely unexplored. In this study, we used a synthesized redox mediator, N-(ferrocenylmethyl)-6-aminohexanoic acid, featuring an extended spacer arm designed to decrease the tunneling distance between the enzyme cofactor and the electrode surface. Sarcosine oxidase and horseradish peroxidase were subjected to bioconjugation via carbodiimide-mediated coupling. The resulting bioconjugates were characterized by cyclic voltammetry, diffusion-kinetic analysis, and high-resolution mass spectrometry following tryptic and peptic digestion. Furthermore, an in silico structural analysis was employed to correlate lysine solvent-accessible surface area with conjugation efficiency. Based on these bioconjugates, a sarcosine biosensor was constructed and tested using human serum as real samples.

item.title: Template-Derived Nickel Oxide Catalysts for Reproducible Oxidative Dehydrogenation of Ethane
item.description:
Abstract
Ethylene, an essential feedstock for many materials, was produced through ethane oxidative dehydrogenation using a template-derived nickel oxide catalyst. A Ni-based metal-organic framework, Ni-BTC, was used as the template, and catalyst preparation was evaluated by varying calcination time, decomposition environment, and preparation timing. These variables were probed to determine the effect on the reproducibility of the nickel oxide catalyst. Samples were characterized using surface area, X-ray diffraction, and thermogravimetric analysis. Findings indicate that template-derived nickel oxide gives reproducible spent-surface-area-normalized ethylene production, with the RSD error minimized to 3.0% compared to 29.0% for the traditional sol–gel preparation method. The best-performing conditions identified in this study were complete air decomposition for 4 h at 400 °C and limited storage time before catalytic testing. Heating the spent catalyst after the reaction provided insight into the effectiveness of the decomposition environments but did not further improve the air-decomposed samples.

item.title: Three Fundamental Challenges in Deep Coal and Gas Outburst: Progress, Controversies, and Future Perspectives
item.description:
Abstract
Coal and gas outburst (CGO) remains one of the most severe dynamic hazards in deep coal mining. Increasing burial depth challenges conventional single-factor criteria. This critical review synthesizes advances in CGO mechanisms reported between 2015 and 2025, focusing on three fundamental challenges: the limited applicability of the 0.74 MPa gas-pressure threshold under deep conditions, the nonmonotonic thermal regulation of gas adsorption–desorption and transport, and the apparent high-storage–low-trigger paradox of tectonically deformed coal (TDC). Comparative assessment of elastic-energy- and adsorbed-gas-dominated theories indicates that deep outbursts are better interpreted as condition-dependent competition among elastic strain energy, gas expansion work, fracture-energy consumption, and dissipative processes. Reported values further show that coal deformation/fracture energy and gas expansion energy can become comparable in magnitude, whereas the fraction of adsorbed-gas energy converted into dynamic work remains highly uncertain. Temperature exerts competing influence on sorption, transport, deformation, and energy redistribution, while TDC combines high gas-storage capacity, low permeability, and low mechanical strength, favoring pressure disequilibrium and structural instability. Three priority research questions emerge: quantifying adsorbed-gas energy conversion into dynamic work, establishing cross-scale similarity and validation for thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) coupling, and developing physics-constrained prediction of nonlinear instability. These advances provide a pathway from single-index hazard identification toward mechanism-informed, multiparameter early warning.

item.title: Site-Selective Oxidative Degradation of the Conserved Disulfide Bridge in Oxytocin and Vasopressin: Chemical Transformations and Structural Destabilization
item.description:
Abstract
Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are major mediators of oxidative stress and represent an important source of chemical instability for biologically relevant molecules, including disulfide-containing peptides. Oxytocin and vasopressin are important signaling neuropeptides whose biological activity critically depends on the structural integrity of a conserved Cys1–Cys6 disulfide bridge. Here, we investigated the oxidative degradation pathways of both peptides under controlled ROS-generating conditions using UV–C irradiation as a reproducible source of radical stress. Structural and chemical changes were monitored by circular dichroism spectroscopy and HPLC–mass spectrometry. Both peptides underwent progressive degradation with prominent modifications of the disulfide bridge, which emerged as a major site of radical attack. Oxidative degradation produced thioether and polysulfide-containing species consistent with disulfide-bridge modification involving cysteine desulfurization and rearrangement, while CD spectroscopy revealed early loss of the disulfide-constrained cyclic structure before extensive degradation occurred. Control experiments employing thiol- and disulfide-reactive reagents further supported the key role of the disulfide bridge in determining peptide susceptibility to oxidative damage. Removal or modification of the sulfur-containing residues significantly altered degradation kinetics and product distribution. These results identify the conserved Cys1–Cys6 disulfide bridge as a major target of ROS-induced degradation in oxytocin and vasopressin under oxidative conditions and provide new insight into the chemical pathways associated with oxidative modification of cyclic disulfide-containing peptides. More broadly, these findings establish a framework for future investigations into whether redox chemistry and oxidative stress contribute to the regulation or dysregulation of oxytocin and vasopressin stability and signaling.

item.title: Heteroaryl-Substituted Secondary Amines as Multifunctional Antimicrobial, Antibiofilm, Acetylcholinesterase, and α-Glucosidase Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
A series of heteroaryl-substituted secondary amine derivatives (6a–g and 7a–g) were synthesized by reduction of Schiff bases obtained in our previous study with sodium borohydride (NaBH4). The molecules were characterized by spectroscopic techniques including 1H NMR, 13C NMR, FTIR, and GC-MS. Following synthesis, all compounds underwent extensive biological investigation, including studies of their antimicrobial, antifungal, antibiofilm, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities, as well as their effects on membrane integrity and molecular docking capabilities. Some molecules exhibited measurable antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida tropicalis. Among the tested derivatives, compound 6a exhibited the lowest MIC90 values against E. coli (749.1 μg/mL) and C. tropicalis (840.2 μg/mL), whereas compound 7d showed the lowest MIC90 value against S. aureus (789.1 μg/mL). In antibiofilm tests, compound 7e maintained high inhibitory activity even at low concentrations, while compound 7b showed the highest single-point biofilm inhibition. Membrane integrity studies revealed significant DNA and protein leakage effects, particularly for compounds 7c and 7g. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) analysis revealed compound-dependent differences in oxidative stress generation, suggesting that ROS production may contribute to the observed antimicrobial effects. In enzyme inhibition studies, compounds 6d and 6f emerged as the strongest AChE inhibitors with IC50 values of 89.17 and 73.35 μM, respectively, while compound 7a showed the strongest α-glucosidase inhibitory activity (IC50 = 173.92 μM). Molecular docking studies provided plausible binding modes and predicted interactions of the selected active compounds within the investigated target proteins.

item.title: Vanadyl Sulfate Embedded in Poly(ethylene glycol) for the Selective Aerobic Aromatic Alcohol Oxidation to Carbonyl Compounds
item.description:
Abstract
A poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based composite containing a well-defined, molecular neutral vanadyl sulfate compound was synthesized in dimethylacetamide (DMA) and characterized. The composite material catalyzed the aerobic oxidation of selected aromatic alcohols to carbonyl compounds in DMA (homogeneous reaction condition) under high selectivity, using a very low amount of vanadium (0.5 mol %). The catalytic activity of the composite material turned out to be significantly superior to that of the bare vanadium compound and to reported catalytic results stemming from vanadyl-based catalyst, which use either high reaction temperature and vanadium loading or toxic and expensive additives (i.e. a TOF value for benzyl alcohol conversion of 57 h–1). PEG turned out to be important not only for the catalytic activity of the vanadium-based catalyst but also for the efficient recovery of vanadium. The deactivation of the molecular vanadium catalyst studied by independent recycling experiments and spectroscopic analyses carried out on the recovered catalyst turned out to be due to the formation of polymeric V(III)-O-V(III) species.

item.title: Sequential Electrochemical Construction of Hierarchical LIG/PPy/MnO 2 Microsupercapacitors with High Areal Capacitance and Device-Level Stability
item.description:
Abstract
Achieving high areal energy storage in flexible microsupercapacitors while maintaining compatibility with direct planar patterning remains challenging, particularly when multiple pseudocapacitive components must be sequentially integrated without compromising electrode accessibility or device level performance. In this paper, we develop a sequential electrochemical construction strategy to integrate polypyrrole (PPy) and manganese dioxide (MnO2) directly onto interdigitated laser-induced graphene (LIG) electrodes without preformed composite powders, slurry casting, or polymer binders. Porous LIG serves as the conductive framework and current collector, followed by in situ PPy electropolymerization and subsequent MnO2 electrodeposition. Systematic control of LIG processing, PPy growth, MnO2 deposition, and gel electrolyte composition establishes a fabrication window that balances electrical conductivity, pseudocapacitive material loading, and structural accessibility while preserving the underlying porous LIG architecture. Stepwise LIG, LIG/PPy, and LIG/PPy/MnO2 controls exhibit the same performance hierarchy at both the individual electrode and complete device levels, demonstrating that the electrochemical gains introduced during sequential functionalization are retained after complete microsupercapacitor (MSC) assembly. The resulting LIG/PPy/MnO2 device delivers an areal capacitance of 621.2 mF cm–2 at 0.37 mA cm–2 and a maximum areal energy density of 55.22 μWh cm–2 at 0.1494 mW cm–2. Extended rate measurements further demonstrate continued electrochemical operation up to 5 mA cm–2 under substantially increased current demand. The device retains 97.04% of its flat state capacitance at 180° static bending, exhibits a device-to-device RSD of 2.29%, retains 94.5% capacitance after 60 days of ambient storage, and maintains 85.1% after 5000 GCD cycles. Series integration further extends the operating voltage from 0.8 to 2.4 V with predictable electrical scaling and enables three MSCs to power a red LED for approximately 183 s. These results establish a directly patterned and independently controlled approach for translating hierarchical pseudocapacitive construction into high areal energy storage, reproducible device performance, and scalable voltage output.

item.title: A Dermal-Epidermal Junction-Inclusive Skin Model Enabled by Controllable Hydrogel Swelling
item.description:
Abstract
Tissue engineered skin models are important tools for the in vitro study of physiological and pathophysiological processes as well as the evaluation of therapeutic strategies and the efficacy of pharmaceutical and cosmetic compounds. Replicating the functional anatomy of cutaneous tissue is a crucial aspect in ensuring that observations made using these models are translatable to the actual situation in native skin. However, most contemporary full-thickness skin models neglect the reconstruction of the undulated microtopography of the dermal-epidermal junction (DEJ), which not only contributes to the biological functionality of the skin (e.g., stem cell niches), but also affects tissue mechanics and drug diffusion. Herein, we fabricated bilayer skin models with DEJ-like microtopographies introduced by interfacial wrinkling between a hydrogel and a nanofibrous membrane through a controllable swelling–deswelling approach. The interfacial wrinkles contributed to the structural integrity of the bilayer models. Their formation could be induced in the presence of living cells through mechanical stress-driven buckling instabilities, thus differentiating the process from commonly used prepatterning techniques. The bilayer models supported the coculture of human dermal fibroblasts and human epidermal keratinocytes and the formation of stratified epithelia. Our findings provide a potential alternative method to introduce DEJ-like anatomical features into full-thickness skin tissue models.

item.title: Valorization of Cannabis sativa Residual Biomass from Industrial CBD Extraction as a Renewable Support for Candida antarctica Lipase B Immobilization and Fatty Acid Esterification
item.description:
Abstract
Residual Cannabis sativa biomass from industrial CBD extraction in ethanol was evaluated as a renewable support for the immobilization of Candida antarctica lipase B (CALB) by physical adsorption, and the resulting biocatalysts were applied to the esterification of long-chain fatty acids with ethanol. Because extractives released by the untreated biomass interfered with protein quantification, three simple pretreatments were compared. Milling alone, with or without buffer washing, gave reproducible immobilization and active, reusable biocatalysts, whereas SDS washing increased protein retention but led to nearly inactive preparations, indicating that protein loading alone does not predict catalytic performance. The milling-only biocatalyst converted two industrial palm fatty acid distillate fractions with conversions comparable to those of Novozym 435, retained more than 80% of its initial conversion after five cycles, and was operated in a continuous-flow packed-bed reactor with conversions of 95% or higher at a residence time of 15 min. These results indicate that this residue is a low-cost, minimally processed support for lipase-catalyzed esterification.

item.title: Valorization of Cellulose Sludge as a Sodium Alginate-Based Bioadsorbent for Bromazepam Removal from Water
item.description:
Abstract
The remediation of benzodiazepine residues from industrial discharge remains a critical environmental challenge due to their chemical stability and neurotoxic potential. In this study, cellulose sludge from the pulp-and-paper industry was successfully upcycled into Ca2+-cross-linked sodium alginate hydrogel beads for the targeted removal of bromazepam (BZP). This work represents the first systematic investigation into BZP sequestration using a waste-derived hybrid hydrogel, at deliberately low concentrations (0.5–5.4 mg L–1), kept as close to environmentally relevant levels as the analytical method allows and within the range reported for point-source pharmaceutical effluents. The beads exhibited a rough filamentous surface and an interconnected 3D porous network characterized by a mesoporous texture (SSA: 9.35 m2 g–1; pore volume: 0.04 cm3 g–1) and an amphoteric surface (pHPZC = 8.04). Kinetic studies revealed a rapid initial uptake reaching an experimental capacity of 0.25 mg g–1 at 180 min, with the Elovich model providing the best statistical fit (R2 = 0.994; AIC = −56.9; BIC = −56.7), consistent with adsorption on energetically heterogeneous sites governed by coverage-dependent rate decay. Because the isotherms were measured in this dilute range, no saturation plateau was reached: the equilibrium data were best described by the Freundlich model at 25 °C and by a linear (Henry-type) model at 35 and 45 °C. The hydrogel beads were efficiently regenerated using 0.1 M HCl, maintaining structural integrity and performance across four consecutive cycles (BZP removal of approximately 13–15% in each cycle, with no systematic decline). This study provides a sustainable, zero-waste strategy for the valorization of abundant industrial residues into functional bioadsorbents, directly supporting circular economy goals for emerging contaminant mitigation.

item.title: Compatibility and Insecticidal Responses of Bacillus thuringiensis in Tank Mixtures with Spray Adjuvants against Spodoptera frugiperda
item.description:
Abstract
The fall armyworm, Spodoptera frugiperda, is a major agricultural pest whose management increasingly relies on Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)-based bioinsecticides. However, tank-mix applications with adjuvants may alter Bt performance. This study evaluated the in vitro compatibility of Bt (Xentari) combined with five commercial adjuvants (Li-700, Fighter, Wetcit Gold, Protac, and Tween 80) and compared the insecticidal responses of these mixtures in laboratory bioassays. In vitro compatibility was assessed using nutrient agar to determine vegetative growth and sporulation, while pH variation was measured in laboratory spray solutions over time. Insecticidal response was evaluated through bioassays on artificial diet with second-instar S. frugiperda, using two complementary approaches: spore suspensions derived from in vitro assays and laboratory assays with spray solutions applied at 0, 2, 6, and 24 h after preparation. Tween 80 increased vegetative growth, whereas Li-700 reduced vegetative growth but enhanced sporulation. Wetcit Gold and Protac completely inhibited Bt development in vitro. Protac reduced solution pH below 2.5, indicating strongly acidic conditions. Under the laboratory conditions evaluated, microbiological compatibility observed in vitro did not consistently correspond directly to the insecticidal responses obtained in the artificial-diet bioassays. All Bt-containing spray solutions resulted in final mortality above 80%. Within the Wetcit Gold treatment, final mortality at 2 h was lower than at 6 and 24 h, while no significant differences among Bt-containing treatments were detected within individual resting times. These findings indicate that microbiological compatibility assays and laboratory bioassays provide complementary information for interpreting Bt–adjuvant interactions.

item.title: Flexible Receptor Docking Provides Structural Models for the Recognition of 2-Amino-heteroaryl-benzothiazole-6-anilide Derivatives by Lck via the CorrEA Method
item.description:
Abstract
Structural models of Lck bound to a chemically diverse series of 62 2-amino-heteroaryl-benzothiazole-6-anilide (AHBA) inhibitors were built to examine how the conformational state of the ATP-binding site shapes the structure-based interpretation of their potency. Docking to the static Lck crystal structure (PDB entry 1QPC) generated plausible complexes for only 54 of the 62 compounds, and produced essentially no relationship between docking scores and experimental pIC50 values, indicating that a single receptor conformation cannot capture how this scaffold is recognized. Receptor flexibility was then introduced through the CorrEA protocol, which cross-docks the series against an ensemble of Lck conformations sampled by molecular dynamics (MD) and, using the measured activities of the series as a reference, selects for each ligand the receptor–pose pair that best accounts for the observed potencies. The resulting ensemble accommodated the entire compound set, overcoming the inability of the rigid receptor to host eight of the derivatives, while preserving the canonical orientation of the AHBA scaffold within the ATP-binding site. The ensemble also recovered the hinge and gatekeeper hydrogen bonds to M319 and T316 expected for ATP-competitive protein kinase (PK) inhibitors, which were only partially satisfied in the rigid-receptor poses. Examination of the selected conformations indicates that the series is accommodated through modest, coordinated rearrangements distributed across the glycine-rich loop, the region beyond the hinge, and the back pocket, rather than through a single dominant conformational change. These models offer an activity-consistent structural framework for interpreting ligand recognition by Lck and a transferable workflow for PKs whose binding sites are conformationally labile.

item.title: Connecting Conformational Landscapes with Bioactivity in Macrocyclic Kinase Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Macrocyclization can improve the selectivity and pharmacokinetic properties of kinase inhibitors, yet the conformational basis of these effects remains incompletely understood. Here, we characterized the structures and conformational ensembles of the clinically relevant macrocyclic kinase inhibitors pacritinib and zotiraciclib using microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED), NMR spectroscopy, and molecular docking. Both compounds populate a set of related macrocyclic core conformations, with additional conformational adaptability arising from changes in aromatic torsion angles and substituent orientations. These conformational adaptations correlate with physicochemical properties relevant to aqueous solubility and membrane permeability. Pacritinib exhibits chameleonic behavior through environment-dependent modulation of its exposed polar surface area, whereas protonation of zotiraciclib generates distinct conformational states stabilized by intramolecular cation–π interactions. Molecular docking indicates that the experimentally determined conformations are compatible with productive binding across multiple kinase targets. Collectively, these findings establish a link between conformational adaptability, physicochemical properties, and polypharmacology in macrocyclic kinase inhibitors, providing insights that may guide the rational design of future macrocyclic therapeutics.

item.title: Fluoride-Free Siloxane Circularity at Room Temperature: Tetrabutylammonium Hydroxide as a Dual-Functional De- and Repolymerization Initiator for Silicone Oils, Elastomers, and Hybrid Coatings
item.description:
Abstract
With increasing EU restrictions on fluoride chemistries and their toxicity related to the potential generation of hydrofluoric acid (HF) as well as their corrosivity, there is an urgent need to develop fluoride-free depolymerization methods to enable safe and sustainable siloxane recycling. In this regard, we here present a fluoride-free, at room-temperature (RT) operating depolymerization method, where tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (TBAOH), identified as a highly effective dual-functional de- and repolymerization initiator, transforms silicone-based elastomers into reusable cyclic siloxanes. Thereby, the solvent/polymer ratio (v/w) is the key for controlling the product distribution: at 10/1 (v/w), the depolymerization mixture shifts from D4-rich to high proportions of byproducts greater than 40 mol % and ultimately stops the process, leaving solid educt silicone at even lower dilutions. Under optimized reaction conditions above a threshold of 0.29/1 (w/w) for the TBAOH/polymer ratio, a relative proportion of up to 88 mol % cyclic siloxanes (D3 to D5), with D4 as the main product, is obtained. This corresponds to 77 mol % absolute NMR conversion into cyclic siloxanes. Additionally, it is worth noting that the fluoride-free, RT operating reaction conditions are effective for a very broad educt scope ranging from linear polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) oils, (filled) Pt-cross-linked silicone elastomers, to inorganic–organic hybrid polymers and coatings. Compared to sodium hydroxide (NaOH) as an alkaline reference, TBAOH affords fewer noncyclic byproducts (12–26 mol % vs 25–30 mol %) and a higher D3 (4–14 mol % vs 1–3 mol %) relative proportion, highlighting its distinct reactivity. Fluoride-free siloxane circularity is demonstrated at RT by two complementary repolymerization routes. Within the first method, TBAOH uniquely acts as the initiator for both the depolymerization and the subsequent anionic ring-opening polymerization (AROP) without prior workup, while the second involves the isolation of cyclic siloxanes followed by base-catalyzed AROP. Thus, this TBAOH-enabled, fluoride-free depolymerization method, which operates at RT, provides tunable product distributions and a broad substrate applicability for practical silicone circularity.

item.title: Moringa oleifera Alginate-Based Beads for Adsorption of Selected Heavy Metals: Preparation, Kinetics, Isotherms, and Reusability Studies
item.description:
Abstract
Moringa oleifera (MO) leaf powder, a low-cost natural resource, has been extensively used for the removal of heavy metals from water. To overcome challenges associated with powdered adsorbents, including difficult separation and low recovery, this study details the synthesis and evaluation of MO-alginate (MO-Alg) bead adsorbents for the adsorption of arsenic, cadmium, iron, chromium, zinc, and lead from oil-polluted aqueous samples. The beads were prepared through ionic gelation using sodium alginate (SA) as an encapsulation matrix with varying MO loadings. SEM analysis revealed that MO-Alg beads were spherical with a rough and cracked surface texture compared to smooth pristine sodium alginate (SA) beads, while XRD analysis confirmed the amorphous nature of both materials. At pH 5, MO (4 g) beads achieved the highest adsorption efficiencies. Kinetic studies followed the pseudo-second-order model, while equilibrium data fitted the Langmuir model for As(III) and Cr(VI) and the Freundlich isotherm model for Cd(II), Pb(II), Zn(II), and Fe(III). The Langmuir isotherm model estimated maximum adsorption capacities of 44.22, 61.11, 41.16, 59.14, 55.22, and 76.69 mg/g for As(III), Cd(II), Cr(VI), Fe(III), Pb(II), and Zn(II), respectively, at 25 °C. Negative ΔG° and positive ΔH° values over 25–45 °C confirmed that the adsorption process was spontaneous and endothermic. Reusability tests demonstrated that MO-Alg (1:1) beads maintained strong adsorption performance after seven regeneration cycles with removal efficiencies above 70% for Pb(II), Cd(II), and Zn(II), while As(III), Cr(VI), and Fe(III) remained effective up to six cycles with efficiencies above 60%. Overall, MO-Alg beads have great potential as an inexpensive sorbent for the removal of toxic heavy metals.

item.title: Carbon Nanofiber-Integrated CuCo-MOF as a Conductive Bifunctional Electrocatalyst for Overall Water Splitting
item.description:
Abstract
The CuCo-MOF/CNF electrocatalyst, with a well-defined microstructure and efficient charge transfer was successfully synthesized through a simple solvothermal method. In the CuCo-MOF/CNF composite, the introduction of CNF can effectively improve the conductivity and provide sufficient active sites for the electrochemical reaction. The CuCo-MOF/CNF composite has excellent bifunctional electrocatalytic activity for the HER and OER reactions. The catalyst really stands out with its great performance, requiring overpotentials of 50 mV for HER and 70 mV for OER at a current density of 10 mA cm–2. The CuCo-MOF/CNF electrocatalyst has low Tafel slope values of 98 mV dec–1 for OER and 131 mV dec–1 for HER, along with low charge transfer resistance, exhibiting excellent operational stability for up to 40 h for both OER and HER. Moreover, the catalyst has relatively large double-layer capacitance values of 8.95 mF cm–2 for OER and 3.47 mF cm–2 for HER, implying that the electrochemically active surface areas are quite large (223.8 cm2 for OER and 86.8 cm2 for HER). Overall, these structural and electrochemical advantages contribute to the superior catalytic performance of the electrocatalyst, providing a novel framework for the development of highly efficient and scalable bifunctional electrocatalysts for overall water splitting.

item.title: Effects of Tiger Tail Sea Cucumber Bohadschia argus on Wound Healing In Vitro and In Vivo Using an Acute Rat Model Infected with Staphylococcus aureus
item.description:
Abstract
Infectious wounds caused by Staphylococcus aureus remain a significant clinical challenge due to delayed healing and increasing antimicrobial resistance, necessitating alternative therapeutic strategies. This study aimed to evaluate the wound-healing potential of the ethanol extract of the tiger tail sea cucumber Bohadschia argus (EEBA) through integrated in vitro, in vivo, and in silico approaches. Phytochemical profiling using LC-HRMS identified 260 metabolites, and 12 prioritized compounds were selected for molecular docking analysis. EEBA demonstrated concentration-dependent antioxidant activity in the nitric oxide scavenging assay and inhibitory effects on protein denaturation, indicating anti-inflammatory potential, although differences compared to controls were not statistically significant (p > 0.05). In an excisional wound model in Staphylococcus aureus-infected Wistar rats, topical application of 1% EEBA accelerated wound contraction and improved macroscopic healing compared to the negative control. Histopathological evaluation revealed reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, enhanced fibroblast proliferation, increased angiogenesis, and improved collagen organization across the inflammatory, proliferative, and maturation phases. Hemolysis testing confirmed good biocompatibility with negligible erythrocyte lysis (<5%). Molecular docking demonstrated favorable binding affinities of selected compounds toward key inflammatory targets, including TNF-α, NF-κB, and FLAP, as well as antibacterial targets relevant to Staphylococcus aureus, namely, DNA gyrase-B, dihydrofolate reductase, and penicillin-binding protein. These findings provide preliminary mechanistic insights into the potential wound-healing and antibacterial activities of EEBA. Overall, EEBA exhibits promising wound-healing activity in an infected wound model through modulation of oxidative stress and inflammatory pathways, with selected metabolites also showing potential interactions with bacterial targets associated with S. aureus infection. These findings support the potential development of EEBA as a natural therapeutic candidate for infected wound management.

item.title: Investigating Ferritin Permeability to Metal-Based Drugs through Molecular Dynamics
item.description:
Abstract
In this study, we implemented a workflow based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to assess whether gold(I)-containing complexes can traverse the C3 channels of human H ferritin and which energetic barriers were at play in the process. By using two example complexes for which an extensive experimental characterization was already available, we observed that classical MD correctly indicated which one could spontaneously pass through the channel. To quantify the ability of the ferritin nanocage to retain the internalized complex, we estimated, through steered MD and umbrella sampling simulations, the Potential of Mean Force (PMF) along the pathway from the interior to the exterior. The results reveal a steep energetic barrier that hinders the exit of the complex once internalized. In contrast, the second complex encounters steric and electrostatic repulsion, which prevents its internalization. Analysis of protein-complex contacts shows that the successful translocation of the first complex is electrostatically guided through a sequence of transient interactions with Asp/Glu residues lining the pore. The comparison of these two complexes demonstrates that the C3 channel of ferritin only attracts positively charged species and that the nanocage creates a strongly asymmetric energy landscape for charged complexes. This provides a mechanistic explanation for experimental observations of loading in ferritin. Overall, the work demonstrates a computational approach for assessing the permeability of metal-based drugs through ferritin channels and offers molecular insight into channel-mediated transport processes.

item.title: Fractionation and Identification of Bioactive Peptides from Camel Skin Hydrolysate: In Silico and Molecular Docking Analysis
item.description:
Abstract
Hypertension and glycemia disorders are severe issues in public health, highlighting the urgent need for the discovery of natural bioactive agents with health benefits. In this sense, the present study examines camel skin gelatin hydrolyzate, obtained using Alcalase (GHA). GHA was first ultrafiltrated, and the low molecular weight fraction (<10 kDa) with the highest in vitro ACE and DPP-IV inhibitory activities (82.75% and 72.5%, respectively) was further purified by reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography. Among the resulting fractions (FI to FV), FIII and FIV were the most potent inhibitors against the ACE activity. Thus, they were analyzed by LC-MS/MS for peptide identification. In silico and peptidomic analyses revealed several novel peptide sequences. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA studies were subsequently performed to investigate the interactions and estimate the binding energies of the selected peptides with ACE and DPP-IV. Among the investigated peptides, GPSGPSGL and GPSGPR showed the strongest energy-binding scores against the studied enzymes with favorable interactions with their active sites. In conclusion, hydrolyzed camel skin gelatin is a promising source of multifunctional bioactive peptides and a potential natural ingredient for the management of hypertension and glycemic disorders.

item.title: Biocatalytic Valorization of Used Soybean Cooking Oil for Furfuryl Esters Production: Effects of Alcohol Feeding Strategy and Water Removal on Immobilized Lipase Performance and Stability
item.description:
Abstract
This study describes an efficient biocatalytic process for the synthesis of furfuryl esters from used soybean cooking oil (USCO). The process involves the hydrolysis of USCO using free Candida rugosa lipase, followed by solvent-free esterification of the resulting free fatty acids (FFAs) with furfuryl alcohol (FA) catalyzed by immobilized lipase Eversa Transform 2.0 (ET2.0). Five supports, including acid-treated rice husks with fine (FRH) and coarse (CRH) particle sizes, commercial and rice husk-derived octyl-functionalized silica, and poly(styrene-divinylbenzene) (PSty-DVB), were evaluated for ET2.0 immobilization by physical adsorption. Among the evaluated supports, PSty-DVB provided the highest immobilized protein loading (31.3 ± 1.1 mg g–1) and the best overall catalytic performance in furfuryl esters synthesis. Using this biocatalyst, FFAs conversion reached approximately 94% within 60 min at 45 °C under solvent-free conditions and with a slight excess of FA (FFAs:FA molar ratio of 1:1.15). The combination of stepwise furfuryl alcohol feeding and molecular sieves for in situ water removal improved biocatalyst operational stability, allowing the retention of approximately 95% of the initial activity after 15 consecutive esterification cycles. These results show that ET2.0 immobilized on PSty-DVB is a suitable biocatalyst for the solvent-free conversion of waste-derived fatty acids into furfuryl esters.

item.title: Polyelectrolyte Nature of Model Colloidal Plastics and Their Impact on Molecular Adsorption
item.description:
Abstract
Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) are pervasive environmental pollutants, yet their interfacial structures and molecular adsorption behaviors remain poorly understood. This study investigates the polyelectrolyte nature of model colloidal micro- and nanoplastics (CMNPs)─specifically polystyrene particles featuring plain, sulfate, or carboxylate surface functional groups─and examines how these features dictate molecular adsorption and electrokinetic properties. Using a combination of in situ dynamic light scattering (DLS), electrophoretic mobility measurements, surface-selective second harmonic generation (SHG) spectroscopy, and by relying on previous theoretical and experimental work, we demonstrate that CMNPs possess a soft, hydrated, polyelectrolyte-rich interfacial layer. This brush-like or “hairy” architecture persists regardless of the specific surface functional group and fundamentally alters particle behavior in aqueous media. Electrokinetic measurements reveal nonclassical trends in electrophoretic mobility under increasing electrolyte concentrations, matching theoretical frameworks for soft colloids while contradicting classical hard sphere models. Furthermore, SHG adsorption isotherms for a model cationic dye (DASPI) show that adsorption affinity is governed by a combination of electrostatic and entropic effects, with hydrogen bonding serving as a strong possibility for carboxylated particles. Notably, the adsorption affinity is less sensitive to electrolyte concentration than predicted by classical models, indicating that volumetric charge density and interfacial hydration are likely the primary determinants governing organic molecule adsorption at the CMNP/aqueous interface. By overturning the conventional view of microplastics as rigid, inert particles, these findings highlight the critical importance of accounting for soft, hydrated interfaces when predicting the transport, environmental fate, and contaminant interactions of plastic pollution in natural waters.

item.title: The Effect of Design Parameters on Yields of 33 Harmful and Potentially Harmful Constituents (HPHCs) in Mainstream Smoke of Large Cigars
item.description:
Abstract
The effect of large cigar (LC) design parameters on the mainstream smoke yields of harmful and potentially harmful constituents (HPHCs) is relatively unstudied. Available chemical analysis research on LCs has focused on tar and a limited number of HPHCs (e.g., nicotine, carbon monoxide, benzo[a]pyrene, acetaldehyde, formaldehyde, and acrolein), while many smoke HPHCs have been largely overlooked. Recently, Cheng et al. reported the smoke yields of 33 less commonly studied HPHCs in 10 LC brands generated by the Canadian Intense smoking regimen (55 mL puff volume, 30 s puff frequency, 2 s puff duration, 100% vent block, if applicable). In this study, we compared their previously reported HPHC yields to cigar design parameters (weight, length, circumference, pressure drop, and calculated density and volume) using simple linear regression to determine if any correlations exist that may support future in-depth study. The impact of each design parameter on individual HPHC yields was evaluated using the slopes and correlation coefficients (r2) of the linear regression lines, with P values indicating the significance of the slope. Cigar weight and calculated volume were positively associated with the yields of tobacco alkaloids (anabasine, nornicotine), carbonyls (acetone, methyl ethyl ketone, propionaldehyde), and some volatile and semivolatile (VSV) organic compounds (ethylbenzene, styrene, 2,3-benzofuran, furan), while also being negatively associated with polyaromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) yields. Cigar length was also positively associated with tobacco alkaloids, carbonyls, and VSVs, but did not influence PAH yields. Like weight and volume, higher cigar circumference was associated with lower PAH and heterocyclic aromatic amine yields, but it only had a weaker positive association with tobacco alkaloids, carbonyls, and VSVs. Calculated density and pressure drop were not associated with any consistent or meaningful differences in HPHC yields. These preliminary and rudimentary results suggest that simple design parameters influence HPHC yields in large cigars in a predictable manner. Having a better understanding of how parameters influence HPHC yields can inform evaluations of the public health impact of large cigars and public communications about their health risks.

item.title: Polymer Solution Entanglement Influences the Mechanical Properties of the Resultant Electrospun Fibers
item.description:
Abstract
Electrospun fibers have a range of applications that rely on specific mechanical properties for optimal function. In this study, we examined the diameter-independent relationship between polymer solution entanglement and the mechanical properties of individual electrospun polycaprolactone fibers. Molecular weights of 35 kDa, 45 kDa, and 80 kDa were used at various concentrations to produce smooth fibers from polymer solutions across a range of entanglement molecular weights. Fibers were pulled until failure using atomic force microscopy, and their mechanical properties were determined. Because of the strong diameter dependence, we selected fibers within a limited range to compare initial modulus, rupture stress, and toughness. Within the same polymer molecular weight, the initial modulus, extensibility, rupture stress, and toughness increased with greater polymer solution entanglement. However, when comparing across polymer molecular weights, we observed that changing molecular weight altered extensibility to a greater degree than adjusting entanglement. The fibers produced from 35 kDa PCL had significantly smaller diameters, around 100 nm, than those produced at higher molecular weights, and their mechanical properties did not change with entanglement. These results suggest that fiber mechanics can be controlled and tailored to specific applications through diameter-independent means by altering entanglement and polymer molecular weight.

item.title: A pH-Responsive Fine Powder Coating Strategy for Simultaneous Taste Masking and Physical Modification of Herbal Extract
item.description:
Abstract
Herbal extracts are widely used as intermediates and fundamental materials in pharmaceutical processing. However, the pronounced drawback in powder flowability and intensely bitter taste present major obstacles to the innovation of herbal-derived oral dosage forms. Here, we report a fine powder coating strategy to overcome these challenges for an internally developed herbal extract that exhibits these drawbacks. By employing a tangential fluidized-bed coater, a composite polymer coating formulation was applied to the extract powder. Such a coating formulation achieved rapid release performance under acidic condition and sustained release performance under neutral condition, confirmed by dissolution and kinetic studies. The effect of coating modification on the extract powder was characterized by powder flowability measurements, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analyses. We further demonstrated the efficacy of the taste masking strategy using an electronic tongue system. Our work provides a practical and feasible paradigm for coating fine herbal extract powders, presenting new perspectives for the development of modern oral dosage forms designed for pharmaceutical powders suffering from similar challenges.

item.title: FTIR-Based Quantification of a Corrosion Inhibitor in Solution: Experimental Investigation and Quantum-Chemical Modeling
item.description:
Abstract
Residual corrosion inhibitor (RCI) monitoring is essential for ensuring the effectiveness of corrosion mitigation programs in oil and gas production systems. Among the available analytical techniques, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) offers advantages such as rapid analysis, minimal sample preparation, and the absence of chemical reagents.
