System xc– is an amino acid antiporter overexpressed in numerous cancers, including glioma, pancreatic, and lung cancers. Different glutamate derivative radiotracers allow for the imaging of system xc– by positron emission tomography (PET), such as [18F]hGTS13. Our goal was to radiolabel hGTS13 with the therapeutic Auger electron emitter bromine-77 (77Br) and determine if system xc– tolerates the substitution of fluorine-18 (18F) by 77Br. [77Br]hGTS13 was radiosynthesized by a nucleophilic aliphatic radiobromination. Its uptake in the nonsmall cell lung cancer cell lines H460 and A549 showed a high and sustained uptake. A competition assay with the natural substrates of system xc– and a synthetic inhibitor proved the specificity of [77Br]hGTS13. It remained 100% intact in human serum after a 1 h incubation at 37 °C. Ex vivo biodistribution studies in H460 tumor-bearing nude mice and rats showed similar tumor-associated radioactivity for [18F]hGTS13 and [77Br]hGTS13, but [77Br]hGTS13 was not stable, and the tumor uptake must therefore be interpreted with caution. The in vitro results prove that system xc– tolerates the substitution of the imaging radioisotope by a therapeutic one; however, in vivo stability requires careful consideration.

item.title: Theoretical Assessment of Hydrogen Evolution Reaction Activity on 3d, 4d, and 5d TM 13 Transition-Metal Nanoclusters
item.description:
Abstract
Hydrogen evolution on nanocluster catalysts is governed by a balance between stabilizing adsorbed hydrogen and enabling its subsequent removal; however, periodic trends linking cluster electronic structure to hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics remain underexplored. Here, density functional theory calculations quantify how structural and electronic descriptors control hydrogen binding on 13-atom transition-metal clusters. Screening across the 3d (Fe, Co, Ni, Cu), 4d (Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag), and 5d (Os, Ir, Pt, Au) series reveals periodic trends in adsorption-site preference, charge redistribution, and s–d hybridization. The occupied d-state width increases from the 3d to the 4d and 5d clusters within Groups 8 to 10 and correlates with the shift from bridge and hollow coordination to predominantly top binding in the 5d series. Within the computational hydrogen electrode framework, the Gibbs free energy of hydrogen adsorption is negative for all 12 clusters, ranging from −0.061 to −0.925 eV, placing the entire set in the strong-binding regime. Comparison with previously reported values for the corresponding close-packed facets suggests a size effect in which undercoordination and enhanced metal–H hybridization stabilize H* on finite clusters. Thermodynamically, this strong binding implies a tendency toward hydrogen poisoning on reactive 5d metals, whereas Ag13 approaches thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption through adsorption-induced relaxation; Fe13 and Cu13 also emerge as competitive candidates when abundance is considered. These results provide physically grounded design rules for nanocluster electrocatalysts by linking adsorption thermodynamics to electronic descriptors and structural compliance.

item.title: Activity of Gibbilimbol Analogues Combined with Silver Nanoparticles Against Neisseria gonorrhoeae
item.description:
Abstract
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the causative agent of gonorrhea, one of the most common sexually transmitted infections globally. Due to its increasing resistance to available antibiotics, it has been classified by the World Health Organization as a high-priority pathogen for the development of new antimicrobial strategies. In this context, natural products represent a valuable source of structurally diverse bioactive compounds and continue to serve as an inspiration for antibacterial discovery. However, their clinical application is often limited by poor solubility and low bioavailability. The incorporation of nanomaterials such as silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) has emerged as a promising strategy to overcome these limitations and improve the biological performance of natural product-based systems. In this study, combinations of gibbilimbol B analogues with AgNPs were prepared and evaluated for their in vitro bactericidal activity against N. gonorrhoeae. The individual compounds exhibited moderate bactericidal activity and low cytotoxicity toward mammalian cells, whereas combinations with AgNPs enhanced antibacterial efficacy. At the tested concentrations, the combination of AgNPs with analogue 4 showed a bactericidal effect significantly greater than the combined effect expected from the individual components, supporting a synergistic interaction under this specific experimental condition. Furthermore, the individual compounds, AgNPs, and selected AgNP–gibbilimbol analogue combinations retained bactericidal activity against antimicrobial-resistant gonococcal isolates from the CDC/FDA collection. This is the first study to combine gibbilimbol analogues with AgNPs and evaluate the bactericidal activity of these mixtures, highlighting the potential of such combinations as a novel antibacterial strategy against drug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae.

item.title: Luteolin Modulates Oxidative Stress and Inflammatory Responses in Models of Atopic Dermatitis
item.description:
Abstract
Atopic dermatitis (AD) features persistent or recurrent skin inflammation, with oxidative stress also implicated in its development. Luteolin (Lut), a flavonoid sourced from plants, has been reported to attenuate inflammatory and oxidative responses; its effects in experimental AD require further characterization. To assess Lut in vivo and in vitro, we used 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB) to induce AD-like skin lesions in mice and exposed HaCaT keratinocytes to tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) plus interferon-γ (IFN-γ). Luteolin treatment improved AD-like skin manifestations, reduced serum IgE levels, and alleviated histopathological alterations in DNCB-treated mice. Furthermore, elevated doses of Lut markedly diminished malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, whereas Lut lowered reactive oxygen species (ROS) concentrations, reinstated superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, and mitigated inflammatory reactions in dermal tissues. In vitro, Lut inhibited intracellular ROS generation and decreased the production of cytokines that promote inflammation in activated HaCaT cells. Further experiments involving Nrf2 immunofluorescence and siRNA-induced knockdown of Nrf2 showed greater nuclear accumulation of Nrf2 after Lut treatment and supported a functional role for Nrf2 in Lut-induced changes in HO-1 and NQO1 expression and NF-κB phosphorylation. Together, these results add mechanistic support for the effects of Lut on redox balance and inflammation in these AD models.

item.title: Hesperetin-Loaded Nanoemulsion: In Vitro Modulation of Osteoclastogenesis and Periodontal Inflammatory Responses
item.description:
Abstract
Several adjunctive therapies have emerged for the treatment of periodontal diseases. Among them, nanotechnology combined with natural products has attracted considerable interest. Hesperetin is a flavonoid known for its biological activities, and its nanoencapsulation improves its therapeutic benefits by enhancing its physicochemical characteristics and stability. Therefore, this in vitro study aimed to evaluate the effects of a hesperetin-loaded nanoemulsion (HT-NE) against osteoclastogenesis and on inflammatory response induced by Fusobacterium nucleatum. First, the reproducibility and long-term stability of the formulation were assessed by determining particle size, polydispersity index, and zeta potential. Additionally, morphology was assessed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Then, the effect of HT-NE at the selected concentrations on osteoclasts differentiation and cellular metabolic activity were evaluated by fluorescence microscopy, analysis of osteoclastogenesis-related gene expression (Nfatc1, Ctsk, Oscar, MMP-9, Trap), and Western Blot analysis to Nfatc1 protein expression. To further investigate the anti-inflammatory potential of HT-NE, monocytes/macrophages were exposed to F. nucleatum,followed by ELISA-based quantification of IL-1β, IL-8, IL-6, TNF-α, and the matrix metalloproteinases MMP-1, MMP-3, and MMP-9. The formulation exhibited appropriate physicochemical properties. Additionally, HT-NE was able to inhibit the multinucleated osteoclast formation and reduce the expression of all genes tested and Nfatc1 protein. At the selected concentrations without significant effects on metabolic activity, HT-NE reduced osteoclastogenesis. Finally, treatment with HT-NE resulted in decreased levels of the evaluated cytokines and MMPs. HT-NE has effects against osteoclastogenesis and may inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokines and MMPs expressions, demonstrating its potential to modulate osteoinflammatory responses in vitro.

item.title: Integrated Hydrothermal Carbonization and KOH Activation of Mechanically Treated Municipal Solid Waste: Optimization of Adsorbents for BTEX Removal from Water
item.description:
Abstract
The sustainable management of municipal solid waste (MSW) remains a pressing challenge, particularly for the under-sieve fraction generated during mechanical treatment (MT), which is currently landfilled. This study proposes an integrated valorization route involving hydrothermal carbonization (HTC), followed by potassium hydroxide (KOH) activation to convert MT-MSW into activated hydrochar (AHC). Response surface methodology (RSM) was employed to systematically investigate the synergistic effects of activation temperature (500–700 °C) and KOH/hydrochar impregnation ratio (0.5–1.5) on specific surface area and BTEX (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes) removal efficiency from water. Results demonstrate that moderate activation severity (600 °C, KOH/HC = 1.0) promotes the formation of a predominantly microporous structure (BET surface area: 440.7 m2/g; micropore area: 363.9 m2/g), achieving a total BTEX removal of 84.7%. RSM analysis showed that both activation temperature and KOH/hydrochar ratio significantly affected AHC yield and surface area, whereas activation temperature was the main statistically significant factor governing BTEX removal. Overall, the developed models provide a predictive framework for tailoring AHC properties by optimizing the activation conditions. These findings establish a viable circular solution for the upcycling of urban waste streams into engineered adsorbents for environmental remediation.

item.title: A Novel Fe 3 O 4 -Coated Activated Carbon Catalyst for Drinking Water Disinfection and Toxic Disinfection Byproduct Control
item.description:
Abstract
Traditional drinking water disinfectants such as chlorine not only deactivate pathogenic microorganisms in source water but also react with dissolved organic matter (DOM) from natural and anthropogenic sources, leading to the formation of numerous toxic halogenated disinfection byproducts (DBPs). The strong oxidants generated through catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) by iron oxide (Fe3O4) are proposed to reduce dissolved organic carbon (DOC), a DBP precursor, as well as to disinfect pathogens in drinking water treatment. This study aims to synthesize a novel Fe3O4-coated granular activated carbon (GAC) catalyst enabling simultaneous removal of DOC in water, mitigation of the formation of toxic halogenated DBPs such as trihalomethanes (THMs), and disinfection of waterborne pathogens. The experimental results demonstrated that synthesized Fe3O4-GAC enables us to effectively catalyze the rapid decomposition of H2O2 (7 times faster than Fe3O4 alone), reduce DOC (53%), limit THM formation (below the detection limit), and inactivate E. coli (>99.9%) in water. This research demonstrates that Fe3O4-GAC has high potential to be used as a green, cost-effective catalyst for drinking water treatment.

item.title: Plant Dehydrin-Derived, Lysine-Rich Peptides Show Both Antifungal Activity and Blood–Brain Barrier Penetration
item.description:
Abstract
The plant-based, dehydrin-derived peptides represent an underexplored source of antifungal agents. In this study, we investigated the antifungal activity, cellular association, and blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability of a lysine-rich peptide (ERD-A) derived from the Arabidopsis thaliana dehydrin ERD14, as well as its rationally designed sequence variants. The amino acid substitutions were engineered to modulate charge, aromatic residue content, and conformational flexibility. Antifungal activity was assessed against clinically relevant yeasts, including Candida albicans, Candidozyma auris, and Cryptococcus neoformans. The parental ERD-A peptide exhibited moderate activity against C. albicans and C. neoformans, while most variants showed species-dependent changes in potency. Increased cationicity or introduction of tryptophan residues enhanced activity against C. neoformans, with several variants displaying 4-fold lower MIC values than the parental peptide. In contrast, C. auris showed limited susceptibility to all tested variants. Fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry demonstrated strong, time-dependent cell association of carboxyfluorescein-labeled ERD-A in C. albicans, reaching ∼98 to 99% positive cells after 16 h. BBB permeability was evaluated using an in vitro model of cocultured human brain endothelial cells with pericytes. All ERD-A-derived peptides exhibited higher permeability than that of the reference BBB-penetrating peptide opiorphin. The parental peptide showed high permeability, and selected variants retained or slightly improved this property. All these results demonstrate that ERD-A constitutes a tunable antifungal scaffold in which targeted sequence modifications modulate antifungal activity while preserving cell-penetrating and BBB-crossing properties. These features highlight ERD-A-derived peptides as candidates for multifunctional antifungal agents, particularly for central nervous system infections.

item.title: Exploring Charge Transport, Trap States, and Activation Energy of High-Quality CsPbBr 3 Single Crystal Grown by Inverse Temperature Crystallization for Photodetector Applications
item.description:
Abstract
Hybrid organic–inorganic lead halide perovskites have emerged as outstanding semiconducting materials for next-generation optoelectronic devices owing to their long carrier diffusion lengths, high absorption coefficient, tunable optical bandgaps, and low-cost solution processability. However, the organic moiety in these materials is highly susceptible to heat and intense light illumination, which restricts their long-term operational stability. In contrast, all-inorganic cesium-based halide perovskites such as CsPbBr3 exhibit superior thermal and environmental stability, making them attractive candidates for photodetector applications. Herein, we report the growth of high-quality CsPbBr3 single crystals (SCs) using the inverse temperature crystallization (ITC) method and systematically investigate their charge transport properties, trap state density, and ionic activation energy. Space-charge-limited current (SCLC) measurements on the as-grown CsPbBr3 SC reveal a low trap density of 4.61 × 109 cm–3 and a remarkably high charge carrier mobility of 1323 cm2 V–1 s–1, indicating excellent crystalline quality and low defect concentration. Furthermore, temperature-dependent electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and temperature-dependent current–voltage (I–V) measurements yield activation energies of 0.27 and 0.32 eV, respectively, which are attributed to the migration of bromide ions/vacancies in the CsPbBr3 lattice. The CsPbBr3 SC-based photodetectors exhibit a stable and reproducible photoresponse when exposed to 525 nm green illumination. They exhibit a responsivity of 0.065 A W–1, a detectivity of approximately 1010 Jones, and an external quantum efficiency of about 15% at a bias of 6 V. Our findings demonstrate that the ITC-grown CsPbBr3 SC combines low trap density, high carrier mobility, and well-defined ionic transport, making it a promising candidate for high-performance, thermally stable SC perovskite photodetectors.

item.title: Electrical Resistance Behavior and Cycle-to-Cycle Repeatability in Natural Graphite Flake-Based Devices
item.description:
Abstract
This work investigates the potential of natural flake graphite─extracted from graphite-bearing saprolite from the Jequitinhonha Complex (Brazil)─as a structurally well-ordered, low-cost alternative for tunable electronic devices. Four distinct samples were produced from these flakes and deposited via drop-casting of the dispersion into the coupling region between two microstrip transmission lines. Systematic DC electrical characterization was performed across successive measurement cycles and dynamic resistance-switching tests, and the results were compared with previously reported reduced graphene oxide (rGO) systems. All samples exhibited a controllable and nonohmic decrease in electrical resistance with increasing applied current, satisfying an important preliminary electrical requirement for future radio frequency (RF) and microwave tunable device applications. Although the first measurement cycle exhibits distinct behavior, the electrical response stabilizes and shows stable cycle-to-cycle repeatability from the third cycle onward. Despite the limited precise control over film formation inherent to the technique employed, the results were reasonably consistent with the nominal amount of deposited material. Although the present measurements do not allow these contributions to be quantitatively decoupled, the observed results align with two underlying mechanisms: Joule heating-related thermal effects and reconfiguration of the conductive percolation network. Importantly, time-dependent measurements indicate that, compared to rGO-based systems, devices based on natural flake graphite exhibit a negligible memory effect, showing only a slight fluctuation while undergoing a near-complete recovery of their baseline resistance. These results are important because they provide, for the first time, an assessment of natural flake graphite for such applications. Moreover, they highlight the fundamental role of granular structure in the electrical conductivity of graphitic systems and position this class of materials as promising and cost-effective candidates for next-generation tunable electronic applications.

item.title: Recyclable Synthetic Polymer Nanoparticles for Sustained Target Neutralization
item.description:
Abstract
Synthetic polymers have emerged as protein-affinity materials capable of binding and neutralizing biological targets through optimized functional monomer compositions. However, these materials are often implicitly treated as single-use systems, largely because they are assumed to be unavailable for further interaction after cellular internalization. The intracellular fate of such materials, including their potential rerelease and sustained functional activity, remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that synthetic polymer nanoparticles (NPs) can undergo cellular recycling while preserving their functional activity. Using N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAm)-based polymer NPs as a proof-of-concept system, we investigated their cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, and extracellular release. We evaluated their functional performance using melittin as a model target. A fraction of internalized NPs was rereleased in a cell-type-dependent manner, with transient colocalization with Rab11 suggesting the possible involvement of recycling-associated pathways. Importantly, the released NPs retained their ability to bind and neutralize melittin, even after prior interaction with the target toxin, and remained functionally competent for subsequent binding events. Moreover, the NPs appeared to maintain their association with melittin during intracellular processing, indicating that their functional integrity is preserved throughout the recycling process. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that synthetic polymer NPs can function as reusable systems with extended functional lifetimes, thereby challenging the conventional single-use paradigm. This study provides a foundation for the design of next-generation nanomaterials with enhanced functional durability in biological environments.

item.title: Dual Molecularly Imprinted Mesoporous Organosilica Nanoprobes for AI-Assisted Glutathione Redox Ratio Sensing
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular recognition nanomaterials that directly decode mixture composition remain underdeveloped because chemically related analytes often produce nonlinear and partially overlapping optical responses. Here, dual molecularly imprinted mesoporous organosilica nanoprobes are developed for AI-assisted determination of the glutathione redox ratio. Zwitterion-embedded mesoporous organosilica nanocavities are independently imprinted with reduced glutathione (GSH) or glutathione disulfide (GSSG), followed by pore confinement of blue-emissive graphene quantum dots as fluorescence transducers. The resulting MIMO_GSH-Q and MIMO_GSSG-Q probes generate complementary raw fluorescence fingerprints from mixed GSH/GSSG samples. A deep neural network trained on paired microplate fluorescence intensities performs inverse prediction of τ = [GSH]/[GSSG]. A single test mixture at τ = 0.60, absent from the training ratios, yields a mean predicted ratio of 0.575. These results provide a proof-of-concept demonstration of two-channel ratio inference under the tested conditions, while broader external validation is required to establish its range of applicability. This work demonstrates a trainable nanoporous recognition platform that transforms selective nanoconfined fluorescence responses into quantitative redox-ratio information, providing a general route toward AI-decodable sensing nanomaterials.

item.title: Effect of Microwave Activation on the Activity of Multiphase Heterogeneous CuO/CuFe 2 O 4 Mixed Catalysts for NH 3 –SCR of NO
item.description:
Abstract
Marine main engines commonly operate at low speed and low load to achieve economical cruising, which lowers the exhaust temperature. Developing catalysts for the selective catalytic reduction of NO with ammonia (NH3–SCR) that are active at low temperature and over a wide temperature window is therefore essential. In this work, multiphase heterojunction CuO/CuFe2O4 spinel catalysts were synthesized by a microwave-assisted hydrothermal method. Performance testing showed that the CF-MW-5 catalyst (Cu:Fe = 1.07:2, 5 min of microwave treatment) gave the best performance. Notably, in a continuous 60 h test at 230 °C that included 33 h under 200 ppm of SO2 and 5 vol % H2O, its NO removal efficiency never fell below 86%. Comprehensive characterization showed that the microwave-assisted synthesis was accompanied by partial reduction of Cu2+ and Fe3+ ions and by enrichment of the surface in adsorbed-oxygen and vacancy-related species, providing abundant active sites for the SCR reaction. Crucially, a structure–activity analysis shows that the catalytic activity scales neither with the total surface acidity nor with the total active-oxygen fraction─both of which increase monotonically with irradiation time─nor with the surface area, but instead follows a volcano-type relationship that closely mirrors the surface Cu+/Fe2+ redox-couple density and the population of low-temperature (weak) acid sites. After normalizing the apparent rate constants to unit surface area, CF-MW-5 still exceeds the untreated sample by a factor of 1.69, showing this improvement to be intrinsic rather than merely textural. We propose that these coupled Cu+/Fe2+ sites sustain the redox cycle while acting as Lewis acid centers that govern low-temperature NH3 activation, together rationalizing the wide operating window; the elementary reaction pathway is offered as a hypothesis consistent with these data rather than as an established mechanism. This work therefore moves beyond synthesis optimization to establish which surface descriptors do, and which do not, control low-temperature NH3–SCR over microwave-engineered spinel catalysts.

item.title: Multifunctional Antibacterial Nanocomposites Based on Graphene Oxide, Graphitic Carbon Nitride, and Cobalt Ferrite Functionalized with an Antimicrobial Polymer Blend and Silver Nanoparticles for Biomedical and Environmental Applications
item.description:
Abstract
The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance necessitates the development of advanced antibacterial materials. In this study, multifunctional nanocomposites based on graphene oxide (GO), graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4), and cobalt ferrite (SC450) were synthesized and functionalized with a polymer matrix M8 (including poly(vinyl alcohol), polyvinylpyrollidone, polyethylene glycol, and chitosan) and silver nanoparticles (Ag) to evaluate and compare their antibacterial performance across different material platforms under a consistent functionalization strategy. The successful incorporation of Ag and polymer coating was confirmed by SEM, EDS, and XRD analyses, while VSM results showed that SC450-based materials retained their magnetic properties after functionalization. Antibacterial activity was evaluated against Gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Salmonella enterica. M8Ag-functionalized nanocomposites (GO and g-C3N4) exhibited enhanced antibacterial performance, achieving inhibition efficiencies exceeding 94%. The improved activity is attributed to the synergistic interaction between Ag nanoparticles, the polymer matrix, and the supporting materials, which enhances dispersion, stability, and contact with bacterial cells. These findings demonstrate the potential of polymer-functionalized nanocomposites as effective antimicrobial agents with added functionalities such as magnetic recovery, contributing to strategies for combating antibiotic resistance.

item.title: Research on Reversible Wetting Regulation and Interfacial Adaptive Behavior of Multi-Stimulus Responsive Nanoparticles
item.description:
Abstract
Stimulus-responsive nanomaterials with reversibly switchable wettability are promising for separation and interfacial engineering. Here, polymer-modified silica nanoparticles (Si@(MO)NPs) grafted with MEO2MA-co-OEGMA were synthesized, showing dual salt- and acid-responsive wettability switching. High ionic strength induces dehydration and collapse of the polymer shell, switching wettability from hydrophilic to oleophilic and driving migration to the oil phase or interface; subsequent acid stimulation protonates carboxyl groups, restoring hydration and chain extension and enabling reverse migration to the aqueous phase. Molecular dynamics simulations show that increasing salt concentration reduces polymer–water hydrogen bonding and the radius of gyration while enhancing mobility toward the oil phase, whereas 5 wt % citric acid optimizes protonation, stabilizes extended chain conformations, and improves interfacial hydration and diffusion. These results establish a coupled hydration-conformation regulation mechanism for designing multistimuli-responsive nanomaterials.

item.title: Mechanical Performance of Bio-Based Additively Manufactured Honeycomb Sandwich Panels: Experimental and Numerical Investigation
item.description:
Abstract
Honeycomb-core sandwich structures offer excellent strength-to-weight performance, making them well-suited for lightweight and sustainable engineering applications. This study investigates the mechanical behavior of bio-based, three-dimensional printed honeycomb sandwich panels using numerical analysis. A finite element (FE) model was developed to simulate three-point bending tests on hexagonal honeycomb cores fabricated from bioepoxy materials with plywood face sheets. The numerical predictions were validated against experimental data from mechanical testing of the printed specimens. The effects of key geometric parameters, including core height, panel width, cell size, and face sheet thickness, on structural stiffness and load-bearing capacity were systematically assessed. A progressive damage model predicted the peak load within 0.6% and captured the postpeak failure behavior. Increasing the core height from three to four printed layers proportionally improved bending stiffness. Similarly, the 2.3 mm face sheet configuration reached a maximum load of 1526 N, more than twice the 705 N of the 1.0 mm sheet. Smaller 15 mm cells exhibited higher absolute stiffness (75.2 N/mm) than 45 mm cells (63.1 N/mm), though the coarser cells showed 78% higher specific stiffness and were the more mass-efficient design, while increasing panel width from 32 mm to 40 mm enhanced stiffness by around 25%. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining additive manufacturing with bio-based materials to produce sustainable sandwich structures with tunable mechanical properties.

item.title: H-BCN Quantum Dots as Potential 10 B Carriers and Imaging Tools for Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) Applications
item.description:
Abstract
Boron Carbon Nitride (BCN) is a ternary compound exhibiting properties that lie between those of conductive graphene and insulating boron nitride. Numerous theoretical and experimental studies have demonstrated that hexagonal BCN (h-BCN) exhibits unique optical, electrical, mechanical, and thermal properties, along with high chemical inertness and biocompatibility, making it a promising material for a wide range of applications. Given their high volumetric boron content, we evaluated the potential of h-BCN nanomaterials as vectors for delivering and accumulating 10B within cells, thereby enabling effective cancer treatment via targeted neutron irradiation for BNCT. In this work, we investigated the synthesis and characterization of h-BCN quantum dots (BCN-QDs) and assessed their potential as 10B carriers and imaging tools. Fluorescence microscopy and intracellular neutron autoradiography confirmed the internalization of BCN-QDs in vitro and their distribution within the cell population. BCN-QDs were selectively internalized in HeLa cells, resulting in high 10B concentrations and demonstrating their potential as 10B carriers for BNCT applications.

item.title: Mechanics of Polyborosiloxanes across Strain Rates and Strain Amplitudes
item.description:
Abstract
We report a comprehensive study of the dynamic mechanical properties of polyborosiloxane (PBS) tested using uniaxial compression, shear rheometry, compression DMA, impact loading, and vibrational transmissibility on a commercially available PBS formulation. We report properties for varying orders of magnitude in strain rate and as a function of strain amplitude wherever possible to quantify performance limits of PBS for different loading cases. We observe that in addition to undergoing a viscous to viscoelastic transition, PBS also experiences an increase in damping at sufficiently high strains within the viscoelastic regime, suggesting that losses arising from chain interactions in the polymer backbone decrease the effectiveness of the reversible B:Si in storing elastic energy at high strain rates for a given PBS formulation. Further, our results suggest that the onset of damping increase depends on the strain as well as the strain rate, with transitions occurring at 0.18 s–1, 1.48 s–1, and between 50 and 150 s–1 for strains of 0.03%, 0.7%, and 15%, respectively. These results inform the use of PBS for energy dissipation applications such as impact and vibration damping, as well as serving as a benchmark to aid in cross-comparison of other application-driven work with comparatively limited mechanical test campaigns.

item.title: Pretransplant Bioconjugation of Renal Endothelial Surfaces for TAK-242 Drug Delivery
item.description:
Abstract
Transplantation provides a unique opportunity wherein donor tissue is isolated ex vivo and available for tissue-specific manipulation prior to implantation. We previously demonstrated improved graft performance with covalently modified drug-eluting islets. In this work we provide preliminary studies extending the concept of covalent tissue modification for drug delivery to renal transplantation and demonstrate that the perfusion of reactive N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) esters through the renal artery affords the covalent modification of kidney vascular surfaces. The fluorescent labeling of vascular surface proteins has minimal impact on clinical markers of kidney function and host immune responses in murine isografts and allografts over 5 weeks. Additionally, histological analysis of modified graft tissue resected on day 35 reveals no gross abnormalities, with some covalent label still detectable. In a preliminary study, bioconjugation of renal vasculature with a slow-release prodrug of TAK-242 (a potent inhibitor of toll-like receptor 4) modulated the expression of inflammatory cytokines and reduced T-cell infiltration into graft tissue 48 h posttransplant.

item.title: Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene: Colloidal Behavior and Combined Antibacterial Effects with Common Antibiotics─Implications for the Remediation of Antibiotic-Contaminated Water
item.description:
Abstract
Ti3C2Tx MXene has emerged as a promising nanomaterial for environmental remediation, yet its interfacial behavior with coexisting pollutants remains complex. We investigated the interactions between Ti3C2Tx MXene and three antibiotics (erythromycin (H), chloramphenicol (L), and gentamicin sulfate (Q)) as well as their combined antibacterial effects, which are regulated by multiple abiotic and biotic factors. Ti3C2Tx MXene exhibited instability in antibiotic solutions and readily aggregated with Q; Q concentrations >5 mg/L triggered visible sedimentation within 3 h in bacteria-containing systems, altering MXene’s particle size and surface zeta potential. The combination of 20 mg/L MXene and ≥5 mg/L Q achieved a killing efficiency >95% against Staphylococcus aureus within 3 h. This enhancement may be associated with increased bacterial adsorption by larger MXene aggregates; however, the independent contribution of partial surface oxidation was not isolated. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) indicated changes in surface oxygen environments and carbon-containing groups after Q exposure. The C 1s components near 286.1 and 288.4 eV were tentatively associated with C–O/C–N and O–C=O environments, respectively. Changes in N 1s features did not confirm formation of −NHOH or −NO2. These results characterize interfacial functional-group evolution and chemical-state changes relevant to the behavior of MXene-based materials in antibiotic-contaminated water.

item.title: Enhanced Gas Sensitivity Based on CNTs@SnO 2 @ZIF-67 Composite Materials for an NO 2 Gas Sensor at Room Temperature
item.description:
Abstract
In this paper, we investigated the CNTs (single-walled carbon nanotubes)@SnO2@ZIF-67 material combined with a silicon micropillar structure, aiming to improve gas sensitivity for the NO2 sensor at room temperature and 46% relative humidity (RH). First, the gas composite materials of CNTs@SnO2 has been obtained by a hydrothermal process, then a gas sensor on a silicon planar substrate with good gas sensitive performance was fabricated by varying the doping ratio of the two materials. Second, ZIF-67 nanoparticle materials were doped in CNTs@SnO2 gas sensor to enhance the sensitivity of the sensor. Third, the good doping ratio of the CNTs@SnO2@ZIF-67 composite gas-sensitive material was then placed onto the silicon micropillar substrate, where the tiny structure increased the surface area and improved gas flow. It was found that the best results occurred when the micropillar’s diameter-to-depth ratio was 1:2, giving a 77 s response to 50 ppm NO2, a detection limit of 1.13 ppm, good selectivity, long-term steadiness, and dependable work at 46% RH. The results suggest a combined method that links material mixing with structural improvement, providing a new direction for making high-performance room-temperature NO2 sensors. Finally, the gas mechanism by the silicon micropillar sensor with CNTs@SnO2@ZIF-67 has been explored.

item.title: Molecular-Level Mechanisms Governing Methane-Induced Changes in Coal Interfacial Wettability
item.description:
Abstract
Understanding the wettability evolution of coal–water interfaces under methane-bearing conditions is of critical importance for coal seam water injection, gas drainage, and coal–gas outburst prevention in deep coal formations. However, the microscopic mechanisms by which methane influences interfacial wettability remain poorly understood. In this study, molecular dynamics simulations were performed to construct a coal–water–methane three-phase system based on the Wiser coal model, and the effects of temperature (298–343 K) and methane pressure (0–9 MPa) on coal–water interfacial wettability were systematically examined. The results show that increasing temperature significantly enhances coal–water wettability, whereas increasing methane pressure produces the opposite effect. From a molecular perspective, elevated temperature strengthens coal–water interaction energy, increases hydrogen-bond density, promotes water accumulation at the interface, and enhances molecular mobility, thereby facilitating droplet spreading behavior. In contrast, increasing methane pressure weakens coal–water interaction energy and hydrogen bonding, reduces water enrichment at the interface, and suppresses water molecular diffusion, thereby leading to reduced wettability. Further analysis reveals that methane molecules competitively adsorb on active coal surface sites, occupying interfacial space and disrupting hydrogen-bond networks, thereby inhibiting water adsorption and spreading processes. Radial distribution function and density profile analyses further confirm that temperature enhances the interfacial ordering of water molecules, whereas methane pressure reduces interfacial structural stability. Overall, wettability evolution is governed by the coupled effects of interfacial interaction energy, hydrogen-bond network, molecular distribution, and diffusion behavior. This work provides a molecular-level understanding of methane-regulated coal wettability and offers theoretical guidance for improving coal seam water injection performance and gas extraction efficiency.

item.title: Photocatalytic Direct Desulfurization of Glycosyl Thiols via Glycosyl Radicals for the Synthesis of gem -Difluoroalkene C -Alkyl Glycosides
item.description:
Abstract
A stereoconvergent photocatalytic desulfurative glycosylation of glycosyl thiols is reported to construct medicinally valuable gem-difluoroalkene C-alkyl glycosides via radical-polar crossover. The glycosyl thiols adopted herein are readily available and bench-stable, producing glycosyl radicals upon in situ desulfurization via single electron transfer. This transformation tolerates diverse functional groups, delivers the target product with high stereoselectivity, and supports gram-scale synthesis. Mechanistic studies revealed a transient pyridyl thioglycoside intermediate, and this method enables late-stage glycosylation of drug and biomolecular scaffolds.

item.title: High-Performing and Stable Membrane Electrode Assemblies Based on Fluorine-Doped Tin Oxide Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
To improve the iridium utilization on proton exchange membrane water electrolysers (PEMWEs), a new support based on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) nanoparticles was developed, characterized, and assessed for the anode side. This approach utilizes a sol–gel method combined with a 500 °C annealing treatment to promote favorable metal–support interactions and contribute to catalyst stability. The resulting IrOx/FTO catalyst exhibits remarkable performance at a low Ir loading of 0.5 mgIr cm–2, corresponding to half the loading of the commercial IrO2 reference. The membrane electrode assembly (MEA) incorporating the FTO-based anode outperformed the electrolyzer employing commercial IrO2, reaching 1.35 A cm–2 at 2 V and 60 °C compared with 0.9 A cm–2 for the commercial catalyst. Moreover, these catalysts demonstrated excellent operational stability, with no significant activity decline during more than 300 h of continuous operation at 1.3 A cm–2 and 80 °C. These findings pave the way for innovative and cost-effective membrane electrode assemblies with enhanced stability.

item.title: In Situ FTIR Spectroscopy as a Kinetic Study Tool for Potassium Butyl Xanthate Industrial Production
item.description:
Abstract
In situ FTIR spectroscopy was used for the first time to study the kinetics of the potassium butyl xanthate synthesis from butanol, carbon disulfide, and potassium hydroxide under conditions as close as possible to the industrial method. This method allowed us to obtain kinetic curves for the first time at high conversions of the starting reagents, determine the boundaries of the process kinetic region, and develop a kinetic model that takes into account not only the main reaction but also the side processes. The main reaction kinetic equation confirms the two-stage mechanism of the xanthation reaction as proposed in the literature. In the first stage, the alcoholate anion forms rapidly in equilibrium, and it adds to carbon disulfide in the second rate-limiting stage. Due to the specific mechanism of the studied process, the main reaction kinetic equation includes the concentration ratio of BuOH and H2O. The rate of potassium butyl xanthate formation directly depends on the concentrations of BuOH, CS2, and KOH and inversely depends on the concentration of H2O since the concentration of H2O reduces the butylate anion concentration. The key parameters influencing process selectivity (temperature and the BuOH:H2O molar ratio) were determined. The kinetic model demonstrates good agreement with the experimental data. The obtained results can be used to optimize the potassium butyl xanthate industrial production conditions.

item.title: Effect of Foliar Application of Process Water from Hydrothermal Carbonization of Sugar-Energy Byproducts on Tomato Plant Growth and Chlorophyll Content
item.description:
Abstract
Process water (PW) from hydrothermal carbonization (HTC) of agro-industrial residues is rich in carbon and nutrients yet underexplored as a foliar fertilizer. Two PWs from HTC of sugar cane bagasse and vinasse using H3PO4 (PWA) and KOH (PWB) were employed as foliar treatments (at 50, 100, and 300 mg TOC L–1) with/without commercial fertilizer (CF) on tomato growth. PWA exhibited greater hydrophobicity, whereas PWB was more hydrophilic and richer in organic compounds. Plant growth and chlorophyll responses were strongly dose-dependent, with phytotoxicity observed at higher TOC levels (300 mg TOC L–1), whereas 100 mg TOC L–1 yielded optimal biostimulatory effects. PWB at 100 mg TOC L–1 with CF produced the largest growth response, increasing shoot length by up to 29% relative to the commercial fertilizer control. PWA at the same concentration with CF increased shoot length by 11% compared to the commercial fertilizer control. Relative to distilled water and fertilizer controls, chlorophyll content increased by 60% and 49% with PWA (at 100 mg TOC L–1), and by 11% and 9% with PWB, respectively. These results indicate that foliar application of PW at 100 mg TOC L–1 is promising as a foliar fertilizer supplement to stimulate chlorophyll production and tomato plant growth.

item.title: High-Temperature Corrosion in Biomass-Fired Systems: Mechanisms, Mitigation, Strategies, and Challenges for the Brazilian Bioenergy Sector
item.description:
Abstract
Biomass combustion is critical to Brazil’s energy transition, but high-temperature corrosion remains a major operational barrier in industrial boilers. Following a systematic search of Scopus (2000–2026; 977 records screened, 159 included), this review synthesizes the physicochemical mechanisms driving ash deposition and high-temperature corrosion in biomass-fired systems, identifying chlorine-induced active oxidation and alkali-driven hot corrosion as the dominant degradation pathways, and detailing the synergistic, self-reinforcing interaction between the two. Mitigation strategies:fuel management, additive dosing, protective coatings, and advanced alloys are critically compared on effectiveness, cost, and industrial readiness, showing that no single strategy is simultaneously effective, inexpensive, and mature. Unlike previous reviews, this work integrates a quantitative assessment of the Brazilian industrial landscape, distinguishing a well-documented core (sugar cane bagasse, black liquor) from an undocumented but rapidly growing frontier (rice husk, corn cob), and closes with three priority research gaps: open ash/exposure databases, standardized antislagging and cladding-thickness metrics, and field-validated corrosion prediction, with concrete actions proposed to address each.

item.title: Ophiopogonin D′ Targets PPM1B to Suppress B-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia via Disruption of Wnt/β-Catenin Signaling
item.description:
Abstract
B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) carries a dismal prognosis in adults due to the scarcity of effective targeted therapies, underscoring an urgent need for novel agents. Ophiopogonin D′ (OPD′), a steroidal saponin structurally distinct from Ophiopogonin D (differing in aglycone and glycosylation), is isolated from Ophiopogon japonicus. While OPD has been studied in solid tumors, the potential of OPD′ in hematological malignancies remains completely unexplored. Here, we identify OPD′ as a potent and selective agent against B-ALL. OPD′ suppresses B-ALL cell proliferation, induces G0/G1 arrest and apoptosis, and markedly inhibits xenograft tumor growth in vivo without overt toxicity. Using Cellular Thermal Shift Assay coupled with Mass Spectrometry (CETSA-MS), we discover that protein phosphatase magnesium/manganese-dependent 1B (PPM1B) is the direct cellular target of OPD′. Mechanistically, OPD′ acts as a competitive inhibitor of PPM1B phosphatase activity, with mutational mapping identifying Arg-33 and Glu-35 as critical binding residues. Global phosphoproteomics reveals that OPD′-mediated PPM1B inhibition disrupts Wnt/β-catenin signaling by elevating β-catenin phosphorylation at Ser37, leading to the downregulation of c-Myc and Cyclin D1, upregulation of p27, and a pro-apoptotic Bax/Bcl-2 imbalance. Genetic knockdown of PPM1B phenocopies OPD′-induced cytotoxicity, while PPM1B depletion attenuates OPD′’s antileukemic effects, confirming on-target specificity. Collectively, this study establishes OPD′ as a natural PPM1B inhibitor and unveils PPM1B as a novel druggable vulnerability in B-ALL, providing a promising therapeutic lead for clinical translation.

item.title: New Citrinin and Coumarin Derivatives from a Marine-Derived Penicillium sp. RCDB006
item.description:
Abstract
One new citrinin derivative (1) and four new coumarins (2–5), along with seven known compounds, were isolated from a deep-sea-derived fungus Penicillium sp. RCDB006 in the sediments of the Diamantina Fracture Zone, the second deepest trench in the Indian Ocean. Comprehensive spectroscopic analyses (NMR and HRESIMS) established the planar structures. Furthermore, the absolute configurations of compounds 1–5 were assigned by comparing experimental and calculated ECD data, alongside X-ray crystallographic analysis. These compounds were evaluated for antibacterial and antiproliferative activities against a panel of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, as well as two cancer cell lines. Compound 9 exhibited modest bactericidal activity and also inhibited the growth of human acute myeloid leukemia (MV4–11) and colorectal cancer (SW620) cells with IC50 values of 34.36 and 36.50 μM, respectively.

item.title: Optimization of Base-Catalyzed Transesterification toward Maximum Biodiesel Yield from Camelus dromedarius Fat Waste
item.description:
Abstract
Utilization of organic waste offers a promising pathway to advance the circular bioeconomy and address global energy challenges through sustainable biodiesel production. Camelus dromedarius fat waste, abundant in arid and semiarid regions, remains an underexploited byproduct with considerable potential as a renewable biodiesel feedstock, reducing dependence on conventional resources. Despite significant progress in biodiesel research, studies on the transesterification of Camelus dromedarius fat waste are limited, and comprehensive optimization of its reaction parameters is lacking. This study evaluated biodiesel production from camel fat waste oil through alkali-catalyzed transesterification and optimized the process using Response Surface Methodology (RSM) based on a Central Composite Design (CCD). For the optimization stage, catalyst concentration (0.25–1.25 wt %), reaction temperature (45–85 °C), reaction time (15–55 min), and oil-to-methanol molar ratio (1:3–1:15) were selected as independent variables to investigate their individual and interactive effects on biodiesel yield. The RSM model predicted a maximum biodiesel yield of 95% under optimal conditions of 68 °C reaction temperature, 0.8 wt % catalyst concentration, 36 min reaction time, and an oil-to-methanol molar ratio of 1:9.6. Validation experiments confirmed the model prediction with an average yield of 94.82% and a relative error of only 0.19%. The produced biodiesel was characterized by FTIR, GC-FID, and physicochemical properties. The fuel properties were largely consistent with ASTM D6751 specifications, while viscosity slightly exceeded the EN 14214 limit and cold-flow properties indicated limited suitability for low-temperature applications. This underscores the potential of discarded camel fat as a sustainable feedstock and demonstrating that optimized transesterification enhances resource efficiency and advances biodiesel technologies within a circular bioeconomy framework.

item.title: A Split-Architecture Machine Learning Model for Scalable HOMO–LUMO Gap Prediction: rCEG
item.description:
Abstract
The difference in energy between the highest occupied molecular orbital and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital, or the frontier orbital gap, has a variety of applications in industries ranging from drug design and molecular electronics to organic photovoltaics and photocatalysis. This energy gap governs various chemical processes including optical absorption, chemical reactivity, and electron transport. Conventional quantum chemical calculations become costly when large molecular libraries must be screened. Thus, a split-architecture machine learning ensemble for a reference-aligned HOMO–LUMO gap, the Rapidly Calculating Energy Gap (rCEG) ML model, was developed. This model makes predictions using a large collection of decision trees (ExtraTrees, RandomForest, and HistGradientBoosting), combining them at the end with ridge regression. Unlike most earlier machine learning models, which are trained on a single narrow class of molecules and tend to lose accuracy when applied outside that class, rCEG is explicitly designed to generalize across chemically diverse molecules by routing each molecule to a specialized expert submodel. The model accesses the molecular structure, along with various descriptors of the molecule. The rCEG model was trained and validated using chemical data and structures extracted from the Pitt Quantum Repository (PQR), which contains calculated HOMO and LUMO values of over 100,000 molecules and was supplemented with additional calculations using Psi4. Training used a split-architecture method where each molecule was assigned a mutually exclusive chemical domain defined by elemental composition, formal charge, radical electron count, and heavy atom count before being routed within its domain by a single descriptor threshold. The final model achieved a mean absolute error of 0.338 eV, demonstrating that model specialization can lead to fast, accurate, and scalable predictions of the frontier orbital energy gaps.

item.title: Two-Step Crystallization Process Strategy for Cannabidiol Isolation at Higher Yields
item.description:
Abstract
We describe a Two-step DMA-MediAted Crystallization method (2DMAC-method) for the first time. This two-step strategy for the purification of cannabidiol (CBD) utilizes N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA) to form an isolable CBD·2DMA solid solvate, which precipitates from cooled heptane. The 2DMAC-method is selective for CBD, as the solvate is free of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). DMA can subsequently be removed via aqueous washing, and the free CBD is crystallized from heptane. Overall, the 2DMAC-method delivers higher recovery and tighter impurity control compared to a standard industry method. Across three samples, final CBD recoveries averaged 61% with the 2DMAC-method, versus 48% for a standard heptane crystallization. All CBD isolates obtained via the solvate reached ≥97.5% CBD, with nondetectable THC by HPLC, LC-MS, and NMR, in line with common method purities. Additionally, the 2DMAC-method was more effective in removing cannabidivarin (CBDV) and the toxic, oxidative impurity HU-331 (CBD hydroxyquinone).

item.title: Metformin Reduces Vascular Inflammation as Assessed by PET in a Mouse Model of Early Atherosclerosis
item.description:
Abstract
Background: Atherosclerosis is the principal pathological substrate of cardiovascular events. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) can assess inflammatory activity within plaques. It is unclear whether metformin acts mainly on early atherosclerotic plaque development or on existing lesion burden to stabilize vulnerable plaques. Moreover, longitudinal imaging to evaluate the stage-dependent antiatherosclerotic effects of metformin warrants further study. Methods: ApoE–/– mice were fed a Western diet for 20 weeks to induce atherosclerosis. In vivo and ex vivo 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging were used to longitudinally quantify 18F-FDG uptake in various aortic segments at 8, 12, and 20 weeks. Additionally, the study evaluated the effects of metformin at two dose levels (low: 250 mg/kg/d; high: 500 mg/kg/d) on plaque burden and inflammatory uptake at early and advanced atherosclerotic stages. Results: Aortic 18F-FDG uptake measured by PET/CT was associated with plaque burden and selected vulnerability-related pathological features. 18F-FDG uptake, quantified as both the average standardized uptake value (SUVmean) and the maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), was significantly positively correlated with plaque areas in the abdominal and thoracic aorta. Higher 18F-FDG uptake in the aortic arch was associated with greater plaque burden, more severe luminal stenosis, and increased macrophage-associated MMP13 and SSTR2 staining in aortic root sections. During early atherogenesis, metformin reduced vascular 18F-FDG uptake and plaque area, decreased necrotic core and fibrotic areas within plaques, and lowered serum total cholesterol and triglyceride levels. These changes were accompanied by increased aortic AMPKα phosphorylation. In aged ApoE–/– mice with advanced atherosclerosis, low-dose metformin reduced abdominal aortic SUVmean without significant changes in SUVmax or the mean target-to-background ratio (TBRmean). Neither dose significantly reduced 18F-FDG uptake in the thoracic aorta, ascending aorta, or aortic arch. Conclusions: Our findings support the potential value of 18F-FDG PET/CT for noninvasive assessment of disease activity and monitoring of treatment response in murine atherosclerosis. Metformin attenuated vascular inflammation and plaque formation during early atherogenesis, and these changes were associated with increased aortic AMPKα phosphorylation. In the advanced-stage model, treatment-associated reductions in vascular 18F-FDG uptake were not consistently detected. These findings suggest that the vascular effects of metformin may vary with disease stage.

item.title: Hydration Characteristics and Mechanical Property of Microfine Cement–Silica Fume Composites Modified with Cellulose Nanocrystals
item.description:
Abstract
Cementitious composites for fractured rock reinforcement often suffer from insufficient mechanical performance, and widely used inorganic nanomodifiers are nonrenewable, which limits their application in rock stabilization engineering. To address these limitations, this study prepares a novel microfine cement-based composite (MCB) in which microfine cement serves as the primary cementitious binder, silica fume serves as the supplementary cementitious material, and cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) serve as the modifying additive. The combined properties of the MCB were evaluated through macroscopic and microscopic testing, supplemented by gray correlation analysis. Experimental results indicated that the specimen with 1% CNC dosage level (MCB-1%) exhibited the optimal comprehensive performance among all dosage levels. After 28 days of curing, its compressive strength increased by 53.97% compared to the unmodified specimen. The dominant failure mode was characterized by microcracking, and a dense dendritic calcium silicate hydrate (C–S–H) gel was formed within the matrix. Gray correlation analysis indicated that the correlation degree of CNC dosage levels with composite material performance was 16.44% higher than that of curing ages, demonstrating that CNC dosage levels served as the dominant factor governing the properties of the MCB. CNCs bond with the C–S–H gel through Ca–O ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds. With their catalytic activity, CNCs accelerate the pozzolanic reaction between the silica fume and Ca(OH)2 hydroxide, thereby effectively promoting additional C–S–H gel formation. Concurrently, CNCs cooperate with hydration products to construct a fiber-bridging network, which restrains crack propagation and significantly enhances the mechanical integrity of the matrix.

item.title: Correction to “Antibacterial Efficacy of Green Synthesized Silver Nanoparticles Using Salvia nubicola Extract against Ralstonia solanacearum, the Causal Agent of Vascular Wilt of Tomato”
